Strategic intelligence · Preliminary · 2026-09-21

Strategic intelligence — preliminary outside-in blueprint

Voes & Co

A founder-run, digitally native vegan footwear brand is preparing to open its ownership to the public through a crowd equity raise at the same moment it needs to prove its AI-assisted marketing, sizing, and manufacturing story can travel responsibly into new geographies without diluting the trust that is its core brand asset.

Prepared for

Desiree Dupuis, Founder & CEO, Voes & Co (role verified verbatim in a cited external source: shoutoutla.com, “Meet Desiree Dupuis | Founder & CEO,” published 2024-07-22)

Prepared by

The Be Human Company

Assessment date

2026-09-21

Status

Preliminary. Not the final blueprint.

Demonstrate the strategic value of a Be Human engagement by exploring how AI-assisted marketing, sizing, and operational-readiness capabilities could support Voes & Co’s stated crowd equity campaign and planned expansion into Australia and Europe.

This preliminary blueprint demonstration draws on the supplied conversation and selected external research. It offers an initial view of opportunities we could explore together. The final blueprint is developed separately once you subscribe or pay for an engagement with The Be Human Company. The ideas here remain preliminary and require internal discovery and validation.

01

The strategic window

Voes & Co is a Vancouver-linked, digitally native vegan footwear brand whose founder describes her goal as building “the world’s first global iconic vegan fashion brand that represents the values of veganism through and through”. On the call analyzed for this package, she stated the brand is “about to launch a crowd equity funding campaign” to fund “a new collection new styles and really scale up the brand and reach bigger markets” (transcript:vos-and-co-desiree-dupuis.txt, ~01:08, E008/E012). This is a founder-stated, forward-looking intention as of the recording; this task’s research did not surface a live or completed crowdfunding filing or platform listing for Voes & Co on the major US or Canadian portals it checked (see Section 10 and Section 11) — the campaign should be treated as planned, not yet publicly confirmed.

Independent research corroborates the founding story and the brand’s current market position. Desiree Dupuis has described the idea for the brand originating in 2016, after running “insurance businesses for 10 years,” and being vegan since 2008 (“When I first learnt about the atrocity of the animal agriculture industry in 2008 I stopped eating and wearing animal products,” shoutoutla.com, 2024-07-22). The brand’s first commercialized product — a Chelsea boot made from Desserto cactus leather sourced in Zacatecas, Mexico — was funded through a Kickstarter reward campaign published 2021-12-09 (kickstarter.com), which independently confirms the “100 pairs of shoes at a time,” low-MOQ manufacturing model the founder describes on the call.

Why timing matters, and where the window is real vs. unproven:

  • Regulatory timing is real and dated. US Regulation Crowdfunding currently caps an issuer’s raise at “a maximum aggregate amount of $5 million through crowdfunding offerings in a 12-month period” (sec.gov, accessed 2026-09-21), and non-accredited Canadian investors on platforms such as FrontFundr “can invest up to CAD $2,500 per offering,” rising to $10,000 under certain conditions (info.frontfundr.com, 2024-07-24). These caps and disclosure obligations are the concrete regulatory scaffolding the founder’s stated plan (transcript E008–E010) will run into, regardless of which jurisdiction or platform she ultimately uses.
  • A direct Canadian peer benchmark exists and is dated. Grounded People, a Canadian vegan footwear brand, “received $2.5 million from Right Season Investments Corp., a Canadian venture capital and advisory firm” (modernretail.co, 2023-01-23) — this is a comparable capital event in the same country and category, useful as a sizing reference for the founder’s own raise, not a claim about Voes & Co itself.
  • A directly relevant footwear equity-crowdfunding comparable exists. Undandy, a Portugal-based custom-shoe brand, ran a Crowdcube equity round; contemporaneous coverage states “Undandy is the first in Portugal to raise capital through Crowdcube” (bdaily.co.uk, 2018-11-23), and the campaign’s own Crowdcube page shows “Total Raised £1,169,980” (crowdcube.com, accessed 2026-09-21) — a useful reference point for what a comparable footwear brand achieved via equity crowdfunding, though the products, geography, and era differ meaningfully from Voes & Co’s plan.
  • The plant-leather category the founder is building on has real volatility, dated 2025–2026. Natural Fiber Welding (maker of Mirum, a competing next-generation leather alternative) announced in September 2025 that “NFW, the next-generation material start up, is to close down following two years of poor performance and job cuts” (ecotextile.com, 2025-09-10), then received a rescue financing reported in January 2026: “Less than six months after announcing it would shut down, the next-gen material maker has received new capital to fund operations” (wwd.com, 2026-01-15). This is a live signal that the category Voes & Co is building its story on is not uniformly stable — a relevant fact for any investor pitch that leans on “the plant-leather revolution.”
  • Consumer sustainability demand is directionally real but has a documented gap. A First Insight survey found “62% of Generation Z survey participants prefer to buy from sustainable brands” and that “Generation Z is also the most willing to pay more for sustainable products (73 percent)” (environmentenergyleader.com / firstinsight.com, 2020-01-14). At the same time, a 2025 Cotton Incorporated Lifestyle Monitor finding — reported identically by two independent outlets — states “In the past year, 67 percent of Gen Z consumers have purchased apparel from the fast fashion powerhouse Shein” (cottoninc.com data via wwd.com and lifestylemonitor.cottoninc.com, 2025-04-18). Stated sustainability preference and actual Gen Z purchasing behavior diverge; a campaign or investor pitch built only on “Gen Z cares about sustainability” risks overstating the reliability of that preference as a purchase driver.

Taken together, the window is real (the founder has a working, capital-light supply chain, a stated funding plan, and a values-forward brand identity that resonates with a documented — if imperfect — generational shift), but several of the specific claims that would anchor an investor narrative (the campaign’s platform and target raise, the exact manufacturing partner and its Brazil location, the “2019 = first plant leathers” history) are either unconfirmed publicly or need softening before they go into investor- or consumer-facing materials. Section 10 lists each item precisely.

02

Strategic opportunities inside the business

Each opportunity below traces to a specific stated signal from the call or an independently verified external fact, with the implication, a hypothesis for expected benefit, and the dependency that would need validation before any specific build.

Opportunity 1 — Make the crowd equity campaign’s underlying materials audit-ready before wider distribution.

  • Signal: The founder is already using AI to draft the campaign’s core document — “with the crowdfunding equity campaign, I was updating my business plan. So of course, I’m like back and forth for a whole weekend with Claude cowork” — and is “about to launch” the raise (transcript, ~01:08, E008). No live or completed public filing for this specific campaign was found in this task’s research (Section 10).
  • Implication: Whichever platform and jurisdiction are ultimately used, Reg CF’s and FrontFundr-style disclosure rules apply, and the SEC confirms “Regulation Crowdfunding offerings are subject to ‘bad actor’ disqualification provisions” and anti-fraud rules (sec.gov, accessed 2026-09-21) — meaning claims made in the pitch (including origin-story and material-history claims — see Opportunity 4) carry real compliance exposure, not just marketing risk.
  • Proposed action (illustrative only): A structured, human-reviewed pass over the business plan and any public-facing pitch materials to separate confirmed fact from founder narrative before wider distribution.
  • Expected benefit (hypothesis): Reduced risk of a factual claim in investor materials being challenged post-launch; more credible diligence conversations with prospective investors.
  • Dependency to validate: The actual platform/jurisdiction chosen, and the current draft of the business plan and offering materials — not shared with us (client evidence requested; see Section 10).

Opportunity 2 — Build a reach/marketing capability sized to the stated “biggest challenge.”

  • Signal: The founder names the same problem twice in different words: “I think just like breaking through the noise of being able to like educate consumers because there is so much noise” and “I think that’s the biggest challenge is just reach. It’s like getting people and landing in a world where there’s a lot of Noise” (transcript, ~07:26, E033/E036). She separately describes wanting “a really strong marketing agent” that could take “a base level skill” (e.g., a junior hire) “up like five notches” (transcript, ~37:00–38:51, E144/E145).
  • Implication: The founder has already identified this as her top operating gap in her own words — this is the single opportunity with the clearest founder pull.
  • Proposed action (illustrative only): Scope what a marketing-support capability would need to do for this brand specifically — likely: coordinate launch timing, asset formats, and copy across channels, while leaving strategy, budget, and tone decisions with a human — before committing to any specific build or timeline.
  • Expected benefit (hypothesis): More consistent campaign output without a proportional increase in senior marketing headcount.
  • Dependency to validate: Any timeline or agent-count figures discussed live on the call (e.g., “a month and a half, maybe even two months to train that agent properly,” transcript ~38:51, E146) were the host’s own general framework, stated as his opinion, not a scoped estimate for this business — they should not be treated as a commitment or a verified fact about Voes & Co (see Section 10).

Opportunity 3 — Pilot AI-assisted sizing/3D modeling tied to a stated returns goal, with a baseline first.

  • Signal: “what we’re definitely going to be using is using like AI modeling so for example like 3D generations for the website to enable like a better shopping experience” specifically “to make someone feel really confident… and make sure that they order the right size so that we decrease the amount of like returns” (transcript, ~13:56, E063).
  • Implication: This is a founder-prioritized, not speculative, initiative — but “decrease returns” is only measurable against a baseline that was not shared with us.
  • Proposed action (illustrative only): Before selecting or building any sizing tool, establish the current return rate and its stated causes (sizing vs. other reasons), since the tool’s value case depends entirely on that baseline.
  • Expected benefit (hypothesis): Lower return-driven cost as the brand adds new SKUs and expands into Australia and Europe, where shoe-sizing standards differ from North America.
  • Dependency to validate: Current return rate, current reasons for returns, and current e-commerce stack (client evidence requested; see Section 10).

Opportunity 4 — Resolve and align the manufacturing/material-sourcing narrative before it travels into investor or expansion materials.

  • Signal: On this call, the founder describes “a fully vegan manufacturing private label partner in Brazil” (transcript, ~08:47, E037) and generic “next generation plant-based materials” (transcript, ~03:12, E016). Independent research found that the brand’s first commercialized, documented product — the Harlow Chelsea boot — was made with Desserto cactus leather sourced from a ranch in Zacatecas, Mexico, not Brazil, per the brand’s own 2021 Kickstarter page (kickstarter.com, published 2021-12-09: “the world’s first pair of chelsea boots made from 100% plant-based Cactus Leather,” material described as “grown” on a ranch “in México, in the state of Zacatecas”). We could not independently confirm the current Brazil-based manufacturing partner’s identity or reconcile it with the 2021 Mexico sourcing within this task’s research budget.
  • Implication: If the brand is expanding to Australia and Europe and wants to keep its “environmentally responsible” positioning (transcript, ~08:47, E045), the manufacturing story needs to be internally consistent and independently defensible — especially since it may appear in investor-facing materials subject to anti-fraud disclosure rules (see Opportunity 1).
  • Proposed action (illustrative only): Document the current manufacturing relationship(s), confirm whether the Mexico-sourced Desserto material and the Brazil-based “next generation” material are sequential, parallel, or the same supply chain described inconsistently, and use that as the factual basis for any expansion planning.
  • Expected benefit (hypothesis): A coherent, verifiable supply-chain story that supports rather than undermines the brand’s authenticity claim (“you’re not going to find out… it’s not all that it says it is,” transcript ~45:13, E166).
  • Dependency to validate: Current manufacturing agreement(s), including partner name and location (client evidence requested; see Section 10).

03

The scalability and economics story

What the call and research directly support: Voes & Co already runs a capital-light operating model. The founder describes contract manufacturing (“I don’t need to have my own warehouse. I don’t have to train shoemakers and artisans to make shoes. I don’t have to like I can contract that all out,” transcript ~08:47, E037/E038) paired with third-party logistics (“3PL, where they will warehouse again, I don’t have to pay for my own warehouse, I don’t have to pay for stock employees,” transcript ~08:47, E038) and low minimum order quantities that let the brand “start out like we built our brand with like 100 pairs of shoes at a time” (transcript ~11:48, E046), compared to historical MOQs that “would be in the thousands” (transcript ~11:48, E047). This is a genuinely lean structure, independently plausible given how contract footwear manufacturing works, and it is the strongest, most concrete asset in the scalability story.

What is not established: any current revenue, unit economics, headcount, or burn-rate figures for Voes & Co. On the call, the host (Shane James) offers a general framework claiming a company of “35 people” could in principle “run” with “six people” using AI (transcript ~38:51, E149) and that “investor money” can go “10, 20 times further” with AI because “labor” is a large share of capital deployed (transcript ~41:25, E152). These are the host’s own general market framing, stated as his opinion during the conversation — not a scoped estimate of Voes & Co’s actual headcount, payroll, or achievable efficiency, and they are not independently verified anywhere in this task’s research. The “35” figure appears only inside this same conversation (host states it, founder engages with a similar magnitude — “seven people versus 35 or 40 people,” transcript ~44:14, E164 — without independently restating her own headcount as fact), with no public corroboration (no company filing, LinkedIn page, or press figure found). We are flagging this explicitly rather than repeating it as a fact about the business (see Section 10, flag carried from V010).

For a use-of-proceeds narrative, the founder’s own stated intent — “the money will be used to launch a new collection new styles and really scale up the brand and reach bigger markets” (transcript ~01:08, E012) — is consistent with the regulatory reality that a Reg CF or FrontFundr-style raise is capped and disclosure-bound (Section 1). We are not in a position to say, and do not invent, what raise size, valuation, or economics would make sense for this business; that requires financial baselines this task does not have.

04

The priority operating capability

Of the opportunities in Section 2, the marketing capability (Opportunity 2) is the clearest priority because it is the one the founder names unprompted, twice, in her own words, as both her hardest problem (“breaking through the noise,” transcript ~07:26, E033) and her most wanted solution (“a really strong marketing agent,” transcript ~37:00, E144).

Illustratively, and only as a concept — not a completed workflow design — such a capability could:

  • Take as inputs: brand voice and visual guidelines, past campaign assets and their performance, the specific product/launch being promoted, and constraints like budget and target geography — the founder herself sketches this: “It probably asks you smart questions like what’s your budget? What like I recommend we start in North America” (transcript ~37:00, E144, paraphrased context).
  • Perform activities such as: drafting a launch-timeline outline, assembling assets in the right formats and sizes across channels, and flagging where human review is required (e.g., any claim about materials, sustainability, or company history — see Opportunity 4 and Section 7).
  • Produce outputs such as: a campaign brief, a draft asset list, and a proposed timeline for human approval — not final creative or final claims.
  • Require human decisions on: final creative approval, budget allocation, and — given the brand’s authenticity-first positioning — a sign-off step for any factual or historical claim before it goes external.

What a paid discovery phase would need to establish before this becomes a real build: the founder’s current tools and workflows in more detail, what “junior hire” role she is picturing pairing it with, and what her actual campaign cadence and channel mix look like today. The training-time and agent-count figures discussed on the call (transcript ~38:51, E146–E148) were offered as the host’s general experience with other clients, not a scoped estimate for this brand, and should not be read as a committed timeline here.

05

Proprietary data and organizational intelligence

Known to exist, based on direct evidence:

  • Product-level customer feedback already lives on the brand’s own site — the live Voes & Co homepage displays customer testimonial fragments such as buttery-soft, walkable, comfortable boots (voesandcompany.com, accessed 2026-09-21, homepage testimonial excerpts). This is a real, if currently unstructured, customer-feedback asset.
  • The founder has direct product-experience data from her own use: “I wore them all last year in Bali. They breathe really well. It’s just really comfortable” (transcript ~05:39, E023) — anecdotal, single-user, but a genuine data point about product performance in a warm, humid climate relevant to any Australia expansion.
  • A prior crowdfunding campaign (Kickstarter, 2021) generated backer and campaign-performance history that the brand controls but that was not shared with us.

Would need to be collected, connected, or assessed (not yet known to us):

  • Current return rates and their stated causes (needed to make Opportunity 3 concrete).
  • Current marketing-channel performance and campaign history (needed to make Opportunity 2 concrete).
  • Current AI-tool usage beyond what was mentioned on the call (WhisperFlow, Claude, ChatGPT — transcript E059–E062), and how (or whether) that usage is currently logged or reviewed.

The learning loop we would want to help build, in plain terms: customer feedback on fit/comfort and sustainability claims feeding directly back into both product design and marketing message testing, so that the brand’s “trusted brand” positioning (transcript ~45:13, E166) is continuously checked against real customer response rather than assumed.

06

Customer, community, and ecosystem intelligence

The brand has a real, if modest, public community asset: the Instagram account @voes_and_co describes itself as “A global movement for women, animals & the planet” with the call-to-action “Something BIG is coming soon, join the waitlist” (instagram.com/voes_and_co, accessed via search 2026-09-21) — language consistent with, but not confirmation of, an impending funding or launch announcement. Follower counts fluctuate and were seen in the low thousands at the time of this research; we treat the specific number as a point-in-time snapshot, not a stable metric.

This is worth naming plainly: the founder’s own stated ambition is to become “as recognizable as the Nike swoosh” for veganism (transcript ~45:13, E167) and to “build the army and that foundation of really loyal, people that are part of the community” (transcript ~45:13, E173). A crowd equity campaign will, by design, convert some of that community into literal shareholders — the founder frames this explicitly: “I want to share the wealth. We’re going to be able to give back to animal sanctuaries” (transcript ~45:13, E169/E170). That shift from “customers/followers” to “shareholders” carries real governance and communication obligations (ongoing investor updates, expectation management) that go beyond a normal social-media community, and we do not assume the brand currently has a formal system for managing that — this would need to be confirmed and, if absent, planned for before or during the raise.

We did not find, and do not assume, any existing formal customer advisory panel, ambassador program with contractual terms, or licensed third-party customer data beyond the brand’s own social channels and site.

07

Human capability and governance

Two governance-relevant risks surface directly from this call and from independent research, and both point to the same recommendation: build a human sign-off step for any claim leaving the building.

  • Historical/material claims risk. The founder states on the call: “the first ones that came out in 2019 were pina tax and deserto. So pineapple leather and cactus leather” (transcript ~03:12, E019). We independently confirmed that Desserto specifically launched in July 2019 (“Since launching Desserto in July 2019, the Mexican textile company Adriano Di Marti has partnered with the likes of H&M…,” ecocult.com, 2022-08-15). We were not able to independently confirm or refute, within this task’s research budget, whether other plant-leather materials predate 2019 — but given how visibly the plant-leather-alternatives category has evolved (and given the near-collapse of a competing material maker reported in 2025–2026, Section 1), we recommend the founder’s marketing and investor materials treat “2019 = first plant leathers” as a claim to soften or qualify rather than state flatly, until it has been checked against the fuller competitive timeline.
  • Compliance-sensitive claims risk. Given the founder’s own description of using AI extensively to draft investor-facing material (“back and forth for a whole weekend with Claude cowork,” transcript ~13:56, E061), and the SEC’s confirmation that Regulation Crowdfunding offerings carry anti-fraud obligations (sec.gov, accessed 2026-09-21), any AI-assisted drafting of investor materials should have a defined human review and approval step before publication — this is a judgment and accountability function that should stay human-led regardless of what tools assist the drafting.

Grounded in what the host says about his own company on this call: Be Human Company’s stated approach is to pursue “deep organizational transformation” so that a client “walks away” with “a whole operating system” rather than a single point solution (transcript ~27:37, E105), and to “take care of people first, make sure we get them the result. If they can’t get them the result, let’s send them somewhere where we can help them get the result” (transcript ~28:45, E107). We ground Be Human’s potential role in those stated commitments; we do not invent specific service deliverables, fees, or timelines beyond them.

08

Recommended sequence and measures of value

An illustrative path — not a committed roadmap:

  1. Paid discovery and baseline measurement. Before any specific build (marketing capability, sizing tool, or manufacturing/expansion planning), a discovery phase would need to establish: current return rate and causes; current marketing channel mix and performance history; current manufacturing partner(s) and their capacity/lead times; and the actual status, platform, and jurisdiction of the crowd equity campaign.
  2. Final blueprint. Once discovery establishes those baselines, a final, paid blueprint would translate the opportunities in Section 2 into a specific, scoped plan — including which capability to build first, what data needs to be centralized, and what governance steps (Section 7) need to be in place before any investor- or consumer-facing AI-assisted content goes out.
  3. Implementation and evaluation (subject to agreed scope). Any build, pilot, or rollout — and its evaluation against the baselines established in step 1 — would follow only under a separately scoped and agreed engagement.

Candidate measures of value to test in discovery (illustrative, not commitments): return rate before/after any sizing tool; campaign turnaround time and output consistency before/after any marketing capability; consistency and defensibility of factual claims across investor and consumer materials; and community-to-investor conversion clarity once the campaign specifics are known.

Key open questions for discovery are listed in full in Section 10.

09 — The future-state thesis and strategic question

Which should come first for Voes & Co — locking down and documenting the manufacturing/material story that will anchor your investor pitch, or building the marketing capability that addresses your stated “biggest challenge” of reach — and how does the answer change once we know the actual scope and timeline of the crowd equity campaign?

If Voes & Co’s manufacturing and material-sourcing story is reconciled and documented, if its marketing capability can turn “breaking through the noise” (transcript ~07:26, E033) from a stated frustration into a repeatable, human-approved process, and if its crowd equity materials are built on claims that hold up under disclosure scrutiny, the brand would be in a materially stronger position to pursue the founder’s own stated ambition — a brand that is, in her words, a “cultural movement” people can trust “when you learn more about more and more about the brand” (transcript ~45:13, E166) — as it scales into new markets. We are not promising that outcome; it depends on decisions and data this preliminary package does not have.

Next step: This preliminary package is a demonstration, not the final blueprint. If it’s useful, the next step would be a conversation about a paid Be Human engagement, where discovery would establish the baselines named in Section 8 and turn these opportunity hypotheses into a scoped, evidence-backed final blueprint.

10

Assumptions and questions to validate

  1. Brand name/spelling (resolved by research, confirm for consistency). Independent research (voesandcompany.com; kickstarter.com; shoutoutla.com) and the transcript’s own explicit spell-out (“VOS stands for Vegan Shoes. So it’s V-O-E-S and it’s VOS and Company,” transcript ~56:26, E214) all point to Voes & Co as the correct brand name, while the call notes and much of the host’s speech use “Vos & Co” and one guest utterance is auto-transcribed as “Vose & Co” (transcript ~01:08, E010). This is not tagged as client evidence requested because research resolved it, but we recommend the client confirm this is the exact name/spelling to standardize across all future materials. (Carries notes flag V009.)
  2. Manufacturing partner and material-sourcing narrative (client evidence requested). The call describes a Brazil-based private-label partner (transcript ~08:47, E037) and generic “next generation” plant materials (transcript ~03:12, E016), while the brand’s own 2021 Kickstarter page documents a Mexico-sourced Desserto cactus-leather product. We could not reconcile these within this task’s research budget. (Related to notes flags V005, V022.)
  3. Crowd equity campaign specifics (client evidence requested). Platform, jurisdiction, target raise amount, and valuation are not publicly confirmed anywhere this task searched; treat as founder-stated and forward-looking only.
  4. Current AI/marketing tech stack and returns baseline (client evidence requested). Needed to size Opportunities 2 and 3 concretely.
  5. Team size and organizational structure (client evidence requested). The “35 people” figure was stated by the host, and engaged with in similar magnitude by the founder (“seven people versus 35 or 40 people,” transcript ~44:14, E164), but is not independently confirmed anywhere public, and per our attribution rules a host statement is never treated as a client fact. (Carries notes flag V010.)
  6. Current geographic sales split and expansion timeline (client evidence requested). The founder states the brand is “mostly in Canada and the United States” today with Australia/Europe as future targets (transcript ~08:47, E043/E044); no revenue split or timeline was shared. (Carries notes flag V011.)
  7. “2019 = first plant leathers” claim needs softening. Desserto’s July 2019 launch is independently confirmed (ecocult.com); whether it was genuinely the first plant leather could not be confirmed or refuted within this task’s budget. Recommend qualifying this claim in any external content. (Carries notes flag V001, V013.)
  8. Founder’s other public ventures (context, not confirmed current status). Public sources also associate Desiree Dupuis with Kove Ocean Foods (a seaweed-based food brand, where sources variously describe her as “VP of Sales and Marketing” who helped launch the brand for Cascadia Seaweed, e.g., folioyvr.com, and elsewhere as a “founder,” e.g., sandranomoto.com) and Ruben’s Shoes Society (a footwear-donation nonprofit, where a 2019 source describes her as “Director of Fundraising,” bcsca.ca, while a 2024 bio calls her a co-founder). We note this only as relevant account context (possible split attention across ventures) — we do not assume or assert her current time allocation, and the exact current title at each organization is unconfirmed.
  9. Ambiguous manufacturing-town figure. “A town of 30. 500 shoe making companies” (transcript ~08:47, E037) is ambiguous as transcribed — unclear if this refers to a town of 30,500 people or 30,500 shoe-making companies. (Carries notes flag V005.)
  10. Unverified host claims carried from the conversation, not treated as fact. Several numeric or historical claims were made by the host (Shane James) as general opinion or anecdote and are not independently verified: a “30 to 40%” existential-risk figure attributed to unnamed philosophers (transcript ~12:46, E052; notes flag V003); “only 7% of all businesses” implementing AI properly (transcript ~20:51, E083; notes flag V004); AI making “investor money” go “10, 20 times further” (transcript ~41:25, E152; notes flag V006); Daniel Priestley’s acquisitions being made “10 times more efficient” in “12, 24 months” (transcript ~42:48, E157; notes flag V007); agent training taking “a month and a half, maybe even two months” (transcript ~38:51, E146; notes flag V014); and “40 agents” being achievable “in three months” (transcript ~38:51, E148; notes flag V016). None of these are treated as facts about Voes & Co in this package.
  11. Metadata gaps. Recording date, upload date, and publication date for the episode are not stated in the supplied materials; some syndication points reportedly show conflicting 2025 vs. 2026 dates for what appears to be the same interview (noted for completeness, not material to the substance of this package).

11

Research basis and sources

This assessment is based on (a) a full read of the supplied transcript (transcript:vos-and-co-desiree-dupuis.txt) and the supplied structured call notes (notes:vos-and-co-desiree-dupuis.notes.md), used only as an attribution index and cross-checked against the transcript itself for every claim carried into this package, and (b) fresh external research conducted for this task (web searches and direct page fetches; exact counts appended by the system after this document).

Direct observations (from the transcript, re-verified at the cited timestamp): the founder’s stated vision, funding plan, operating model, AI usage, and growth challenges, all cited inline above with timestamps and (E###) locators.

Strategic intelligence · Preliminary · 2026-09-17

Strategic intelligence — preliminary outside-in blueprint

Birch Bark Coffee Company

A federal Indigenous-procurement mandate, an escalating Canada–U.S. tariff cycle, and an unresolved First Nations water crisis are converging in the same season Mark Marsolais-Nahwegahbow is deciding how far to push Birch Bark’s institutional and retail growth — the window for turning “storytelling and word of mouth” into a systematic institutional pipeline is open now, but it will not stay open on its own.

Prepared for

Mark Marsolais-Nahwegahbow, Founder, Birch Bark Coffee Company Inc.

Prepared by

The Be Human Company

Assessment date

2026-09-17

Status

Preliminary. Not the final blueprint.

Demonstrate the strategic value of a Be Human engagement by exploring how Birch Bark Coffee Company could convert its mission-driven brand and existing institutional relationships into a more deliberate, less improvised growth engine.

This preliminary blueprint demonstration draws on the supplied conversation and selected external research. It offers an initial view of opportunities we could explore together. The final blueprint is developed separately once you subscribe or pay for an engagement with The Be Human Company. The ideas here remain preliminary and require internal discovery and validation.

01

The strategic window

Mark told Shane James on The People Driven CEO Podcast that Birch Bark grew “kind of like went through the floodgates” without a pitch deck, marketing strategy, or business plan (transcript:birch-bark-coffee-mark-marcello-wegwans.txt, ~05:23; E025–E026), that the company had recently moved its roasting relationship from the Atlantic region to Ontario for cost and distribution reasons (~16:59; E058–E069), and that a food-insecurity initiative was still “behind the scenes” and not yet launched (~18:48; E073–E074). Those are direct statements from the conversation, not independent verification.

Three dated, external developments sharpen why now matters:

  • Trade policy is actively squeezing the U.S. market Mark said he wants to re-enter. The Coffee Association of Canada’s own trade bulletin (fetched 2026, most recent entry dated July 22, 2026) shows the U.S. imposing new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods effective August 19, 2026 — weeks before this conversation — layered on top of a volatile 2025–2026 tariff cycle that included a Supreme Court ruling against certain IEEPA-based tariffs (Feb. 2026) and a temporary coffee-tariff removal in late 2025 that was subsequently reversed. Mark’s comment that “with the trade wars, it’s been a bit hard to get the coffee over there” (~01:11:54; E245) is corroborated by this timeline, not merely asserted. This is recent enough to matter directly to any near-term U.S. expansion decision.
  • The founding mission — clean water in First Nations communities — remains unresolved, not historical. Indigenous Services Canada’s own advisory tracker (fetched this task, page last modified September 1, 2026) lists dozens of active long-term boil-water and do-not-consume advisories across Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Ontario, several issued as recently as 2024–2025. This is a direct, current government source, not an estimate, and it means the brand’s founding story is not a completed chapter — it is an active, ongoing claim on customers’ and partners’ attention.
  • Federal and corporate Indigenous-procurement commitments are a live institutional tailwind. Indigenous Services Canada’s own reporting describes a “Mandatory Minimum 5%” federal Indigenous-procurement target introduced in 2021 to give Indigenous businesses more opportunities in government supply chains — a policy signal that aligns with Birch Bark’s own newly worded wholesale positioning, which now explicitly pitches “Indigenous procurement commitments and reconciliation goals” to “corporate offices… government departments and agencies… hospitals and healthcare facilities” (birchbarkcoffeecompany.com/pages/wholesale, fetched this task).

Mark also described a large, unstructured personal investment in AI tools for research, drafting, and social content (~49:30–01:03:29; E165–E220) and Shane framed a broader claim that “only 7% of all businesses… [are] implementing AI properly” (~01:03:29; E210). That statistic is Shane’s own claim as host, not a verified external fact, and is treated here only as a conversational data point, not as evidence about Birch Bark specifically.

Distinguishing sources: the tariff timeline and water-advisory data are direct government/industry-source observations made during this task. The institutional-procurement tailwind is a documented federal policy. The AI-adoption framing is host commentary and is treated as a hypothesis, not a client fact.

02

Strategic opportunities inside the business

a) Formalize the institutional/office-coffee channel around Indigenous-procurement compliance. Signal: Birch Bark’s own wholesale page now targets “corporate offices and boardrooms, universities and colleges, hotels and hospitality, government departments and agencies, hospitals and healthcare facilities” and explicitly ties purchase decisions to “ESG reporting” (birchbarkcoffeecompany.com/pages/wholesale, fetched this task) — a direct evolution from the ad hoc growth Mark described in the transcript (~22:39–26:34; E089–E103), where “everybody came to me” rather than a deliberate sales motion. Implication: the federal 5% Indigenous-procurement target and growing corporate ESG commitments create a demand pull Birch Bark is already positioned for but has not, by Mark’s own account, systematically pursued. Proposed action: explore (in paid discovery) whether a repeatable qualification and documentation process for government/enterprise coffee bids could reduce the trial-and-error Mark described in the institutional-placement economics below. Expected benefit (hypothesis): more predictable, potentially higher-margin institutional revenue, reducing reliance on inbound word of mouth alone. Assumption to validate: current win rate, actual contract volume with named partners (Compass Group, Sodexo, Aramark, Café Van Houtte), and margin structure are not publicly documented and were not confirmed beyond partial secondary mentions (see Section 10).

b) Prepare a launch story for the food-security initiative (Wiisiniwin) now, before it goes live. Signal: Mark said in the conversation that food insecurity work was happening “behind the scenes” and “not yet launched” (~18:48; E073–E074). [Editor’s correction, 2026-09-17: the draft originally asserted this had since launched, citing a quote about a second 5% revenue stream. That quote does not appear on the wholesale page. The company’s own Foundation page instead states: “We are working toward a second stream of giving for campus food security. It is not running yet. When it is, we will say so here. Its name is Wiisiniwin.” Wiisiniwin is a named, planned initiative — still pre-launch, consistent with what Mark said on the recording — not a live program.] Implication: the founder’s own words and the company’s own site agree Wiisiniwin has not launched yet. That is itself the opportunity: a launch-ready growth story (metrics framework, campus-procurement narrative, and distribution plan) could be built now so it is ready the moment the second giving stream goes live, rather than assembled after the fact. It would complement the company’s existing footprint of “over 35 universities, colleges, and schools” (birchbarkcoffeecompany.com/pages/wholesale, fetched this task), close to the “about 40” Mark cited in conversation (~01:11:54; E244). Proposed action: consider (subject to discovery) preparing Wiisiniwin’s story and campus-procurement pitch ahead of its actual launch, so it can ship day-one rather than be retrofitted. Expected benefit (hypothesis): stronger differentiation in campus food-service bids against Tim Hortons/Starbucks-style incumbents Mark contrasted himself with (~01:07:47; E230), realized as soon as Wiisiniwin is live rather than months after. Assumption to validate: Wiisiniwin’s actual launch timeline, planned participation model, and funding mechanism are not publicly disclosed and are a clear discovery question — confirm directly with Mark before building any pitch around it.

c) Build the retail “Indigenous aisle” advocacy into a data-backed retailer pitch. Signal: Mark stated a clear ambition — “let us populate one aisle… where the planogram says here’s all Indigenous food” (~01:06:14–01:07:47; E223, E226) — and described actively challenging Costco on rotation policy (E229) while working with organizations he named as “CCIB” and “Canadian Council of Indigenous Business” (~01:07:47; E228), which corresponds to the Canadian Council for Indigenous Business (ccib.ca). Implication: Costco’s Fall 2024 launch of Birch Bark (CoffeeTalk, Sept. 17, 2024, prior research) and the CCIB relationship (confirmed as a “CCIB Member” on the company’s own site, fetched this task) are real building blocks for this ambition, but no public evidence was found of a retailer adopting a dedicated Indigenous aisle. Proposed action: discovery could assess what evidence (sales data, consumer research, other CCIB member outcomes) would make this pitch land with a national retailer. Expected benefit (hypothesis): permanent, non-rotational shelf space rather than the “checkmark” placement Mark described being stuck with earlier in the company’s history (~16:58–16:59; E060–E061). Assumption to validate: no retailer commitment currently exists; this is Mark’s stated goal, not a confirmed retail outcome.

d) Treat U.S. re-entry as a monitored, not immediate, opportunity. Signal: the Coffee Association of Canada’s tariff timeline (fetched this task) shows a volatile, still-escalating trade environment through mid-2026, directly corroborating Mark’s own comment about trade-war friction (~01:11:54; E245). Proposed action: rather than push U.S. expansion now, discovery could define what tariff or policy conditions would need to change before re-entry makes economic sense, and prioritize the domestic institutional and retail channels described above in the meantime. Expected benefit (hypothesis): avoids repeating the earlier lesson Mark described from over-committing to the Atlantic-region roasting arrangement before understanding the full cost structure (~09:53–16:59; E058–E069).

03

The scalability and economics story

Birch Bark is already structurally capital-light on the production side: Mark said early on he “couldn’t afford a roasting machine” and chose e-commerce over brick-and-mortar for that reason (~09:53; E040), and the company’s roasting is now handled by Reunion Coffee Roasters, described as “a Certified B Corporation” (birchbarkcoffeecompany.com/pages/wholesale, fetched this task; partnership also reported by CoffeeTalk, Sept. 2024, prior research). That means the scaling challenge Mark actually described was not manufacturing capacity — it was demand-side economics.

Mark was candid about this: placing coffee in a single institutional “cafe section” cost roughly $1,500 up front, with no return in year one and a roughly two-year payback (~42:10–43:13; E145–E147). He said that multiplying this across “40” locations forced him to “restructure” his entire financial plan (~43:13; E148–E149). This is a useful, self-reported illustration of how institutional growth without a systematic qualification process can strain capital faster than expected — precisely the risk a more deliberate approach to Section 2(a) is meant to reduce. We do not have Birch Bark’s actual margin, headcount, or financing data, and none is invented here; a paid engagement would need to establish these before recommending any specific capital plan.

04

The priority operating capability

Based on the evidence above, the highest-priority capability to explore is an institutional-opportunity monitoring and qualification capability — a way of continuously tracking where Birch Bark’s mission and certifications intersect with active buying signals (government and university procurement notices, corporate ESG commitments, tariff and trade developments affecting cost structure), and turning that into a short list of qualified conversations rather than waiting for inbound interest as described throughout the transcript (~22:39; E087–E088).

Illustratively, such a capability would draw on inputs like public procurement postings, university sustainability commitments (the kind Humber College’s own sustainability office described when it adopted Birch Bark in 2022 — humber.ca, fetched this task), and trade-policy bulletins; it would produce short briefing summaries for Mark or his team to review; and the decisions about which opportunities to pursue, how to price them, and how to represent the brand in a pitch would remain entirely human-led. This is a concept for discussion, not a specification — what data sources are trustworthy, what internal capacity exists to act on the output, and what it would cost to build and maintain are all questions a paid discovery phase would need to answer.

05

Proprietary data and organizational intelligence

Known to exist (per the conversation and public sources): a multi-year list of institutional and retail relationships (roughly 35–40 universities and colleges, Sobeys, Loblaws, Costco, the Toronto Zoo, and named foodservice partners); Fairtrade and organic certification records; a founder speaking-engagement history (including a documented CCIB “Lightning Talks” appearance in Toronto on Feb. 26, 2026, per Anishinabek News, fetched this task); and one confirmed, live giving mechanism — up to 5% of net income annually to the Birch Bark Coffee Foundation (per the company’s own wholesale and Foundation pages, fetched this task). [Editor’s correction, 2026-09-17: a second stream, Wiisiniwin (campus food security), is named and planned but explicitly not yet running, per the company’s own Foundation page — it is not a live “further 5%,” and no public source describes its funding mechanism yet.]

Would need to be collected or connected: current, itemized totals for Foundation distributions (no public totals were found — this was flagged as a gap by prior research and remains one after this task’s search); Wiisiniwin’s actual launch timeline and funding mechanism once it exists; a record of which institutional bids succeeded or failed and why; and any retailer response, formal or informal, to the Indigenous-aisle pitch Mark described. None of this data was available in the supplied sources or public search, and discovery would need to start by establishing whether it exists internally at all.

06

Customer, community, and ecosystem intelligence

The most relevant feedback loops are institutional and community-based rather than shareholder-based — this is a privately held company with no evidence of external investment or a shareholder base found in this research. Existing relationships worth exploring for structured feedback include university sustainability offices (as reflected in Humber’s own account of why it chose Birch Bark — humber.ca, fetched this task), the seven Indigenous-serving organizations supported through the Birch Bark Foundation, and Birch Bark’s own CCIB membership network. Any use of these relationships for structured feedback or co-marketing would need explicit consent and a clear data-ownership agreement with each partner; none is assumed here, and Birch Bark’s Foundation-supported charities and campus partners were not confirmed to have any existing data-sharing arrangement with the company.

07

Human capability and governance

Mark was explicit that his voice, not an automated one, should represent the brand: “I train it to really understand who I am as an individual, as a human. And I tell them that I do not want an AI approach. I want my approach” (~49:30; E174). He also described consulting elders before finalizing product names (~29:34; E119) and framing the Seven Grandfather Teachings as the foundation’s guiding structure (birchbarkcoffeecompany.com/pages/founder-mark-marsolais-nahwegahbow, fetched this task). Any future capability — including the institutional-monitoring concept in Section 4 — should keep relationship judgment, pricing decisions, cultural and Elder consultation, and public storytelling firmly with Mark and his team; the role of any outside capability is to surface information and reduce manual search effort, not to make commitments on the company’s behalf.

Be Human’s own host, Shane James, frames his company’s mission as helping people “practice their humanity” and describes building internal capability around AI cost management and content production for his own operation (~55:45–01:03:29; E182–E220). Those are the host’s statements about his own company, not commitments made to Birch Bark, and any specific Be Human deliverable would need to be defined and agreed as part of a paid engagement.

08

Recommended sequence and measures of value

An illustrative path — not a committed plan — would start with paid discovery to establish a baseline: current institutional contract volume and economics, actual Foundation/Wiisiniwin distribution totals, and Birch Bark’s real exposure to further U.S. tariff escalation. From that baseline, a final blueprint could define which of the opportunities in Section 2 to prioritize. Any implementation or evaluation phase beyond discovery would depend on agreed scope and is not promised here.

Candidate measures of value to test during discovery include: institutional/government contract win rate, campus footprint growth against the “over 35” figure now published by the company, dollars distributed through the Foundation and Wiisiniwin per year, and any measurable retailer response to the Indigenous-aisle pitch. Key discovery questions include those listed in Section 10.

09 — The future-state thesis and strategic question

As federal Indigenous-procurement targets and an unpredictable tariff environment both reshape who institutional and retail buyers choose to work with, what would it take for Birch Bark’s mission-driven story — not just its coffee — to become the default, evidence-backed choice for every buyer with a reconciliation or ESG commitment?

These changes, if pursued and validated, could support an organization where Birch Bark’s institutional relationships are built on a repeatable, documented case rather than word of mouth alone; where the Wiisiniwin campus food-security story is as visible to procurement decision-makers as the coffee itself; and where the Indigenous-aisle ambition Mark described is backed by evidence a retailer can act on. None of this outcome is guaranteed, and it depends on validating the assumptions in Section 10.

Next step: We would welcome the opportunity to discuss a paid Be Human engagement to investigate this question directly with Mark and his team — starting with the institutional-opportunity and Wiisiniwin visibility opportunities identified above, and the internal data questions in Section 10 that a full discovery phase would need to resolve. The final blueprint would follow only after that engagement is subscribed to or paid for.

Work With Be Human AI →

10

Assumptions and questions to validate

V002: Mark’s claim that coffee is “the second most sold commodity in the world” (~05:23; E027–E028) was used by him as a founding rationale but is stated without a cited methodology or timeframe; it should be treated as his own framing, not verified market data.

V003 / V004: The transcript’s water-mandate timeline is internally uncertain — Mark says “634 nations” (~09:53; E044) and gives conflicting recollection of a 2018-vs-2021 completion target (~09:53; E043). Canada does have roughly 630+ recognized First Nations bands, and government trackers (fetched this task) confirm long-term advisories remain active into 2026, but the specific 634 figure and exact original mandate date were not independently confirmed and should not be repeated as precise facts.

V007: The $1,500-per-location institutional placement economics and two-year payback Mark described (~42:10–43:13; E145–E149) are self-reported and not corroborated by any institutional contract document; treat as illustrative of a pattern, not a current, verified cost figure.

V015: Mark’s statement that he “works with all the big players, Sodexo, Aramark, Compass Group” (~25:23; E103) was not independently confirmed to a documented contract in this research; a Compass Group social post referencing a Birch Bark partnership surfaced in prior search results but was not independently fetched and verified in this task.

V019 (resolved this task): “CCIB” is confirmed as the Canadian Council for Indigenous Business (ccib.ca), and Birch Bark’s own site displays a “CCIB Member” logo (fetched this task) — this flag is now resolved as a verified fact rather than an open question.

Unresolved from prior research and still open after this task: exact current Foundation Fund and Wiisiniwin distribution totals; current headquarters, team size, and organizational structure beyond “Founder”; any confirmed retailer commitment to a dedicated Indigenous product aisle; and current U.S. distribution status given the 2026 tariff escalation. The prior research’s explicit negative findings — no evidence of a Dragons’ Den appearance, no evidence of a Walmart Canada partnership — were not contradicted by any primary source re-fetched in this task and remain binding as open questions, not facts.

New hypothesis, not verified: that a more systematic institutional-opportunity qualification capability (Section 4) would materially improve win rate or reduce capital strain; this requires discovery-stage validation against real bid data Birch Bark has not made public.

11

Research basis and sources

This assessment draws on four supplied sources — the podcast transcript, the structured evidence-notes index (used only to verify transcript timestamps and speaker attribution, never cited as a fact source), a prior research report on this same client (treated as authoritative prior research per its role), and a raw prior-sources evidence file — plus a fresh, limited round of external verification conducted during this task (5 web searches, 6 page fetches, 0 GitHub calls, 0 vision calls). Where the prior research and this task’s fresh research could conflict, the prior research’s findings and explicit negative findings govern unless a primary source was re-fetched directly in this task, which occurred for the Foundation percentage figure and the Humber College partnership (both confirmed as facts rather than estimates). [Editor’s correction, 2026-09-17: the original Wiisiniwin percentage claim was not actually corroborated by the cited source — see Section 2(b), Section 5, and the Citation Check correction above.]

Direct observations from primary sources fetched in this task include the company’s own wholesale and founder pages, Indigenous Services Canada’s advisory tracker, the Coffee Association of Canada’s tariff timeline, Humber College’s news page, and Anishinabek News. Estimates and inference are labeled as such throughout, and strategic recommendations are labeled as hypotheses pending paid discovery.

THE BE HUMAN COMPANY — positioning as described by host Shane James on The People Driven CEO Podcast: a company oriented around “motivating and inspiring people to practice their humanity,” pursuing long-term, relationship-first change rather than short-term transactional wins.

Strategic intelligence · Preliminary · 2026-09-20

Strategic intelligence — preliminary outside-in blueprint

Birch Bark Coffee Company

converting reconciliation-era institutional and retail demand into growth infrastructure that does not depend entirely on one founder’s personal bandwidth.

Prepared for

Mark Marsolais-Nahwegahbow, Founder, Birch Bark Coffee Company

Prepared by

The Be Human Company

Assessment date

2026-09-20

Status

Preliminary. Not the final blueprint.

Demonstrate the strategic value of a Be Human engagement by exploring how Birch Bark Coffee Company could scale its institutional, retail, and reconciliation-driven growth without over-relying on the founder as the sole negotiator, spokesperson, and systems-builder.

This preliminary blueprint demonstration draws on the supplied conversation and selected external research. It offers an initial view of opportunities we could explore together. The final blueprint is developed separately once you subscribe or pay for an engagement with The Be Human Company. The ideas here remain preliminary and require internal discovery and validation.

01

The strategic window

Birch Bark Coffee Company was built, by the founder’s own account, on an unconventional premise: coffee as a vehicle to fund clean-water and Indigenous-community messaging, launched without a pitch deck or business plan and grown through e-commerce because a roasting facility was unaffordable at the outset (transcript:birch-bark-coffee-mark-marcello-wegwans.txt, Mark Marsolais-Nahwegahbow, ~09:53; E028). That path has since scaled into a national footprint: partnerships with the major institutional foodservice operators Sodexo, Aramark, and Compass Group, placement in roughly 35–40 Canadian universities and colleges (birchbarkcoffeecompany.com wholesale page states “35”; the founder states “about 40” on the call — transcript:birch-bark-coffee-mark-marcello-wegwans.txt, ~01:11:54), national retail listings including Sobeys/Safeway and, as of 2024, roughly 33 Costco locations, and a 2026 addition at the Toronto Zoo’s food and beverage outlets (LinkedIn/Toronto Zoo, cited below).

Two dated external developments make this a live strategic window rather than a steady state. First, the federal government’s mandatory minimum 5% Indigenous-procurement target (effective April 1, 2022) has pushed Indigenous businesses to over $1.24 billion in federal contracts in fiscal 2023–24 (6.1% of total value), and large corporates are increasingly matching that benchmark — a structural tailwind for an Indigenous-owned supplier positioned for institutional and government-adjacent buying (mltaikins.com, Mar 27 2026; tbs-sct.canada.ca). Second, the “Buy Canadian” response to renewed U.S. tariff pressure has been documented as resurging through 2025 and into 2026, with Canadian consumers and institutions reporting strengthened resolve to prioritize domestic and Canadian-owned suppliers (CBC, Aug 27 2026; theconversation.com, Mar 3 2025; Bank of Canada, Feb 27 2026). The founder independently describes the mirror image of this dynamic — U.S. expansion becoming harder “with the trade wars” (transcript, ~01:11:54) — which is consistent with, though not proof of, the broader tariff environment reported externally.

At the same time, the founder describes the capital and operating strain of scaling: a single institutional coffee-service placement can cost roughly $1,500 to install, a seven-spot deal can run near $10,000, payback takes about two years, and “where I’m at now is times that by 40,” forcing him to “restructure” plans he had not built capital assumptions around (transcript, ~42:10–43:13; E143–E149). The strategic window, in plain terms: reconciliation-era institutional and retail demand is arriving faster than the founder’s personal capacity to negotiate, finance, and represent every deal — and faster than any documented system exists to plan for it.

02

Strategic opportunities inside the business

Opportunity A

Formalize the institutional-contract economics

Opportunity B

Build the retail “permanent shelf” case

Opportunity C

Move from personal AI experimentation to a governed capability

Opportunity D

Capture the founder’s mentorship and referral network as a company asset

03

The scalability and economics story

Two structural choices already support scale without requiring the company to own capital-intensive infrastructure. First, the founder chose not to build brick-and-mortar or owned roasting capacity from the outset because a roasting machine was cost-prohibitive (“we’re talking millions of dollars here,” transcript, ~09:53); the company instead operates on an asset-light, white-label/branding model (“the brand was the biggest part, the biggest piece… white labeling… it’s a more economical way,” transcript, ~26:34–29:34). Second, the company’s public materials describe current production as roasted in Canada by Reunion Coffee Roasters, an independently certified B Corporation and family-owned specialty roaster (birchbarkcoffeecompany.com wholesale page; bcorporation.net), which is broadly consistent with the founder’s account of relocating roasting to a Toronto-area partner after finding Atlantic-Canada shipping too costly to scale (transcript, ~09:53–16:59). This structure — brand and relationships owned by the company, production capacity owned by a certified partner — is a reasonable basis for capital-efficient growth, but it also means growth economics are tied to a partner’s capacity and terms that were not independently reviewed in this preliminary pass.

The blended-batch approach to sourcing (consistent flavor profile across every bag, rather than variable micro-lot sourcing, per the founder’s account at transcript ~29:34) supports the household-name ambition the founder states directly (“Household name,” transcript, ~01:06:12) by making the product suitable for large-volume institutional and retail buyers rather than a niche specialty audience. Fundraising, headcount, and financial baselines were not discussed on the call and are not estimated here; any scalability model would need the unit-economics data requested in Section 2 and Section 10 before quantifying capital efficiency claims.

04

The priority operating capability

The highest-priority capability implied by the evidence is not a single AI tool but a coordinating layer for institutional and retail growth decisions — something closer to a shared “opportunity ledger” than a finished system. Illustratively, such a capability could:

  • Take in signals the founder already tracks informally — new institutional inquiries, retail conversations, procurement-target deadlines, speaking/reconciliation-outreach requests — in one place rather than in memory and email.
  • Apply a documented cost/return framework (once built per Section 2, Opportunity A) so that a new seven-spot university proposal or a new retail chain conversation can be evaluated against known payback assumptions rather than discovered mid-negotiation.
  • Produce a short, standard “reconciliation and results” case (certifications, foundation impact, sell-through, institutional footprint) that can be reused across retail and institutional conversations instead of rebuilt from scratch each time.
  • Retain human decisions at every commitment point: which institutional deals to pursue, how to price speaking engagements, and how to negotiate shelf placement remain the founder’s calls, informed by better-organized information rather than replaced by automation.

This is a concept for paid discovery to test, not a specification. What discovery would need to establish: which of the founder’s current AI or spreadsheet habits are worth formalizing first, what data actually exists versus needs to be collected, and who besides the founder would use or maintain such a system.

05

Proprietary data and organizational intelligence

Data known to exist, based on the call and public materials:

  • An institutional account footprint (roughly 35–40 universities/colleges per the company’s own wholesale page and the founder’s estimate) and named foodservice partners (Sodexo, Aramark, Compass Group) (transcript, ~25:23; birchbarkcoffeecompany.com).
  • Retail distribution points (Costco, Sobeys/Safeway, and as of 2026 the Toronto Zoo) that are publicly documented (see Section 11 sources).
  • Certification history (Small Producers Symbol, then Fairtrade Canada/organic/100% Arabica) (transcript, ~29:34; ised-isde.canada.ca, Oct 28 2021).
  • A foundation (“we created a foundation,” transcript, ~16:59) whose specific programs and disbursement figures were not detailed on the call.

Data that would need to be collected or assessed before it becomes a usable asset: per-account cost and revenue detail, retail sell-through, actual current AI tool usage and any privacy practices, and the scope of the founder’s informal referral network described in Section 2. None of this financial or operational detail was independently verifiable from public sources and is flagged for client documentation in Section 10.

06

Customer, community, and ecosystem intelligence

The company’s public materials show customer testimonials citing both product quality and the cause (“supporting an Indigenous owned company that was using some of the profits to address the underlying boiled water conditions on many First Nations reservations,” per a testimonial published on birchbarkcoffeecompany.com) — evidence of an existing values-driven customer feedback loop, though it is a small, self-selected set of published reviews rather than a systematic listening program. The founder describes two other ecosystem relationships worth noting: membership in the Canadian Council for Indigenous Business (CCIB), confirmed independently (ccib.ca), and university student associations that the founder says drove early institutional demand by lobbying their own food-service providers directly (transcript, ~24:36–25:23). Any effort to formalize customer or community intelligence would need explicit consent and clear ownership of what is collected — the company does not appear, from available evidence, to already operate a structured customer or community data program, and none should be assumed.

07

Human capability and governance

The founder is currently the sole visible decision-maker for the relationships that matter most: negotiating with major retailers and foodservice operators, setting and defending speaking/consulting fees (“You’re a multi-billion dollar company… you can’t afford to have me come in,” transcript, ~01:09:19), and representing the company publicly. That concentration is a strength (authenticity, speed, trust) and a risk (bandwidth, continuity). Judgment that should stay human-led includes: which institutional or retail deals to pursue, how to price and represent the company publicly, and how community/cultural elements of the brand (naming, Elder consultation referenced by the founder at transcript ~29:34) are handled — these are not tasks to delegate to automation. What could be clarified without displacing that judgment: who else, if anyone, should have visibility into contract economics or scheduling so decisions do not depend solely on the founder’s personal memory and calendar. Consistent with the seller’s own stated orientation — helping people “practice their humanity” and treating technology as something that should work “through the entire org” rather than as a bolt-on to one person’s workflow (transcript, Shane James, ~38:24 and ~01:03:29) — any Be Human role here would be to help structure decision rights and information flow around the founder, not replace his relationships or judgment.

08

Recommended sequence and measures of value

An illustrative path, not a committed plan: paid discovery would first establish a factual baseline — current institutional account list and contract terms, retail placement terms, actual AI tool usage, and foundation program detail (see Document requests) — before any blueprint work proceeds. From that baseline, a final blueprint could explore the unit-economics model (Opportunity A), the retail value case (Opportunity B), a governed AI approach (Opportunity C), and documentation of the referral network (Opportunity D). Implementation and evaluation, if pursued, would follow as separately scoped work.

Candidate measures of value to test in discovery, not promises: number of institutional accounts evaluated against a documented payback model before commitment; retail accounts with confirmed non-rotation or long-term terms; time the founder spends personally re-deriving information he has already gathered once; and the scope of businesses reached through a documented referral network. Key discovery questions include: what does an average institutional install actually cost and return today, what are current retail contract terms, and what does the founder most want to stop having to hold in his own head.

09 — The future-state thesis and strategic question

As institutional and retail demand for Birch Bark Coffee grows faster than one person can personally negotiate, price, and represent, what information and decision-support does the founder need close at hand — without turning the relationships and cultural judgment that built the brand over to anyone or anything else?

If the reconciliation-era procurement tailwind and Buy-Canadian momentum documented in Section 1 continue, Birch Bark Coffee Company’s future state is plausibly one where “household name” (the founder’s own stated ambition, transcript ~01:06:12) is underpinned by systems — cost models, a documented referral network, retailer-ready evidence — rather than by the founder’s individual memory and negotiating stamina alone. This is a hypothesis about direction, not a guaranteed outcome.

Next step: This preliminary view is built from a single conversation and public research; it is not a diagnostic and not the final blueprint. We would welcome the chance to discuss a paid Be Human engagement to validate these opportunities against your actual account, cost, and contract data and develop the final blueprint from there.

Work With Be Human AI →

10

Assumptions and questions to validate

Name/transcription accuracy: The supplied recording renders the company and founder’s names phonetically throughout (“Bridge Bark,” “Birchberg,” “Mark Marcello-Wegwans”). This blueprint uses the names confirmed by independent sources (Birch Bark Coffee Company; Mark Marsolais-Nahwegahbow). Treat any other proper noun in the transcript (e.g., the roaster contact “Adam”) as unverified — no independent source confirmed this individual’s name or role.

Founding date ambiguity: The founder states “Back in the end of 2008, March 2018… I can’t recall” regarding both the founding trigger and the water-mandate deadline (transcript, ~01:43, ~09:53). External sources (CBC, Feb 22 2023; ised-isde.canada.ca, Oct 28 2021) place company founding in 2018; this blueprint treats 2018 as the better-supported date but flags the founder’s own uncertainty.

Notes-register flags carried forward (per source protocol): V001–V003 indicate the underlying evidence-register extraction for parts of this transcript was incomplete (“budget_exhausted”). Direct reading of the full transcript was used to compensate, per the required workflow. V004 (water symposium), V005 (values/roots metaphor), V006 (coffee-naming/Elder consultation), V008 (word-of-mouth vs. social media), V009 (“Household name”), and V011 (Sobeys/Loblaws/Toronto Zoo) were flagged by the notes pipeline as “not found,” but each was independently located and verbatim-confirmed in the full transcript during this task and is cited accordingly above. V007 (a “change civilization at scale… 100 years” statement) was correctly excluded from client claims: direct transcript verification shows this statement was made by the host, Shane James, not by the founder, and is therefore host context, never a client fact. V010 and V012 were not relied upon in this draft.

Institutional and retail figures (client evidence requested): exact current cost and payback per institutional install (the $1,500/seven-spot/$10,000/two-year figures are the founder’s own recollection); current count and list of institutional accounts (35 per company site vs. “about 40” per founder); current retail contract/rotation terms with Sobeys, Costco, and Loblaws (Loblaws presence was stated by the founder but not independently confirmed in this task’s research).

AI usage (client evidence requested): no documentation of current AI tool selection, cost, or data-handling practice exists beyond the founder’s own description; before recommending governance, actual current usage should be inventoried.

Foundation impact (client evidence requested): the foundation’s specific programs and disbursement amounts were not described on the call and were not found in this task’s research.

Speaking/consulting revenue (client evidence requested): the founder describes at least one high-value speaking engagement that fell through over fee disagreement (transcript, ~01:09:19–01:11:00); scope and frequency of this revenue line is unknown.

Roaster partnership terms (client evidence requested): the current supply relationship with the Toronto-area roaster is corroborated in outline by public company materials (Reunion Coffee Roasters) but no contract terms were reviewed.

11

Research basis and sources

This assessment draws on the supplied podcast transcript (transcript:birch-bark-coffee-mark-marcello-wegwans.txt) read in full, its associated evidence-register notes file (notes:birch-bark-coffee-mark-marcello-wegwans.notes.md) used only as an attribution index per the required protocol (never cited as a source of fact), and external web research conducted for this task. Direct observations are claims stated by the founder on the call and independently corroborated where noted; external findings are drawn from company materials, government sources, and press with URLs and dates below; estimates and strategic inference are labeled as such throughout (e.g., the priority-capability concept in Section 4, and the future-state thesis in Section 9). No financial figures, headcounts, or ROI were invented; all specific numbers either come directly from the founder’s account (flagged as such) or from a cited external source.

THE BE HUMAN COMPANY

Strategic intelligence · Preliminary · 2026-09-14

Strategic intelligence — preliminary outside-in blueprint

Cheekbone Beauty

A decade of Shopify purchase history and a first skincare launch meet an abrupt new U.S. tariff: the next twelve months will test whether Cheekbone’s small team can turn data it already owns into faster, values-aligned decisions.

Prepared for

Jenn Harper, Founder and CEO, Cheekbone Beauty

Prepared by

The Be Human Company

Assessment date

2026-09-14

Status

Preliminary. Not the final blueprint.

Demonstrate the strategic value of a Be Human engagement by exploring how Cheekbone Beauty’s existing customer-data work and AI-tool adoption plans could be organized into a durable operating capability at the exact moment the business is absorbing a new U.S. tariff shock and launching its first skincare product.

This preliminary blueprint demonstration draws on the supplied conversation and selected external research. It offers an initial view of opportunities we could explore together. The final blueprint is developed separately once you subscribe or pay for an engagement with The Be Human Company. The ideas here remain preliminary and require internal discovery and validation.

01

The strategic window

Three things are converging on Cheekbone Beauty in the same narrow window, and the conversation this blueprint is based on happened right in the middle of it.

First, a tariff shock that hit a real revenue line. On July 20, 2026, the U.S. government announced a new 50% tariff on a range of Canadian-made goods, including cosmetics, effective August 19, 2026 (BNN Bloomberg, July 26, 2026; Cheekbone Beauty blog, July 28, 2026). Jenn Harper told BNN Bloomberg/CP24 that the U.S. market represents about 20% of the business, which she described as having four full-time employees. Cheekbone’s own blog post is direct about the consequence: “for the products we manufacture here in Canada, a 50% tariff makes it financially unworkable for a business our size to keep shipping directly to the United States,” and the company paused direct-to-U.S. shipping of Canadian-made goods starting August 19, while continuing to route through retail partners JCPenney and Amazon US (Cheekbone Beauty blog, July 28, 2026). This followed an earlier, opposite signal: in spring 2025, “Buy Canadian” sentiment had driven a 52% year-over-year sales increase (January–April) with a 190% surge in March, prompting Harper to say she was “pivoting to building her customer base in Canada first” (Yahoo Finance/Financial Post, May 18, 2025). In other words, the same trade dynamics that boosted Cheekbone in 2025 have, by mid-2026, become a direct threat to a fifth of its business. This is dated, verified, and directly relevant — not background noise.

Second, a first-ever category launch. After what Harper describes as roughly 12 years in the beauty space and about a decade making color cosmetics, Cheekbone launched its first skincare product, the Restorative Barrier Serum Stick, in the week of August 26, 2026 (Cheekbone Beauty blog, “Skincare: The Next Evolution of Cheekbone Beauty,” Aug. 26, 2026, by Jenn Harper).   • Proposed action: Assess what it would take to refresh the segmentation on a defined cadence (e.g., quarterly) and assign clear internal ownership, so it functions as a living input to marketing and demand decisions rather than a point-in-time report.
  • Expected benefit (hypothesis): Faster, evidence-based reallocation of marketing spend and inventory planning as U.S. shipping direct-to-consumer pauses and skincare demand is still being learned. This is a hypothesis; Cheekbone has not stated whether or how the analysis is currently maintained.
