Strategic intelligence · Preliminary · 2026-09-20

Strategic intelligence — preliminary outside-in blueprint

Cheekbone Beauty

is pushing into a first skincare product line after twelve years of color-cosmetics formulation, while its founder is publicly signaling a CEO succession search — a moment when leadership continuity, ingredient-claim substantiation, and customer-data governance will determine whether the brand’s Indigenous-rooted trust position scales into the next product category and sales channel.

Prepared for

Jen Harper, Founder and CEO, Cheekbone Beauty

Prepared by

The Be Human Company

Assessment date

2026-09-20

Status

Preliminary. Not the final blueprint.

Demonstrate the strategic value of a Be Human engagement by exploring Cheekbone Beauty’s leadership-transition, category-expansion, and AI/data-governance opportunity as it moves from a decade of color-cosmetics operation into skincare and omnichannel retail.

Note on naming: this package follows the spelling used in the supplied interview transcript (“Jen Harper”) throughout. Public company materials and independent press consistently render the name “Jenn Harper.” Both refer to the same founder/CEO of Cheekbone Beauty; see Section 10.

01

The strategic window

What the conversation establishes directly. In her own words, Jen Harper describes Cheekbone as “a color cosmetics company” that in August “launched our first skincare SKU… after… the last 12 years developing color formulas” (transcript:cheekbone-beauty-jen-harper.txt, Jen Harper, ~00:54; E003). In the same conversation, she also states Cheekbone “will celebrate 10 years of business this November” and, later, responds “10 years in” when the host congratulates her. She separately states, describing the brand’s origin, “I think even when we launched in 2016, is the idea of how business is done”. She also says she is “probably looking for” a new CEO “in the near future,” while she would prefer to be “chief product operating officer”.

What fresh research adds. Multiple independent sources — Cheekbone’s own site, an industry trade podcast (Glossy), a Canadian government small-business case study, and a national magazine — consistently place Cheekbone’s founding idea in January 2015 and its official brand launch in November 2016:

  • “In January of 2015, Jenn Harper had the most vivid dream of little Indigenous girls covered in colorful lip glosses. That dream is what gave birth to Cheekbone Beauty…” (cheekbonebeauty.com/pages/about, undated, accessed 2026)
  • “Harper launched Cheekbone Beauty in Nov. 2016 as a DTC brand.” (glossy.co, 2023-04-13)
  • “In 2016, Jenn Harper founded Cheekbone Beauty, the first Indigenous cosmetics company in Canada.” (ised-isde.canada.ca, 2021-07-04)
  • “In 2016, despite no experience in cosmetics, Jenn founded Cheekbone Beauty…” (chatelaine.com, 2022-04-19)

Counting from a November 2016 official launch, November 2024 would be the brand’s eighth anniversary, not its tenth. Counting from the January 2015 “dream” origin story, November 2024 is closer to nine years and ten months — colloquially roundable to “10 years,” which is a plausible (but unconfirmed) reconciliation. This is a real, source-supported tension inside the guest’s own statements and against independently corroborated company history, not merely an inference — see Section 10 (V008).

A second, related timing question: the claim of “12 years developing color formulas” before an August 2024 skincare launch would place formula development around 2012, before even the January 2015 origin story and the November 2016 launch date that Cheekbone’s own materials and independent press consistently report. This is an internal arithmetic tension in the guest’s statement, not something fresh research resolved either way (Section 10, V002/V003).

Why timing matters regardless of the exact anniversary. Two dated, verifiable developments intersect with Cheekbone’s skincare move: (1) the U.S. cosmetics regulator’s Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022 expanded record-keeping and facility-registration requirements but “did not ban any additional chemicals,” leaving “clean” undefined and the U.S. banning only “eleven chemicals… while the European Union has banned more than 2,400” (University of Cincinnati Law Review, 2024-03-06); and (2) active U.S. class actions challenge “clean” labeling at exactly the kind of retailer Cheekbone already sells through — Finster v. Sephora USA Inc. and Boyd v. Target Corp. (cited in University of Cincinnati Law Review, 2024-03-06, citing court complaints filed 2022 and 2023 respectively). Cheekbone itself makes claims in this exact space — “we will not allow silicones, petroleum-based ingredients in any of our formulas” and products that are “biodegradable when they reach back into an ecosystem” (transcript, Jen Harper, ~00:54; E006, E004) — while also stating, correctly per the external record, that “there is no global or regulatory body that can define clean”. Moving into skincare — a category with more active/functional ingredient claims than color cosmetics — while this labeling-litigation climate is live is a genuine, dated reason the timing matters, independent of which anniversary is correct.

02

Strategic opportunities inside the business

Each item below traces to a specific signal; each is a hypothesis for paid discovery, not a finding.

Opportunity A

Substantiate “clean”/biodegradable claims before skincare scales

Opportunity B

Formalize leadership succession and institutional-knowledge transfer

Opportunity C

Govern the AI-driven customer-data capability as it scales

03

The scalability and economics story

Cheekbone’s own public materials, independently reported, show a company that has already diversified beyond a single channel: launch as a “DTC brand” in November 2016 (glossy.co, 2023-04-13), a first proprietary product (Sustain Lipstick) in March 2020 funded in part by a $350,000 convertible-debt investment from Raven Indigenous Capital Partners that had grown to “almost $2 million” by April 2023 (glossy.co, 2023-04-13), an online Sephora Canada launch in September 2021 followed by placement in five physical Sephora stores by November 2021 (glossy.co, 2023-04-13; newswire.ca, 2021-09-21), and, as of April 2023, a Thirteen Lune marketplace and roughly 600 J.C. Penney store-location partnership (glossy.co, 2023-04-13). This is a genuinely omnichannel model, not a pure-DTC one — a correction worth noting against any framing (including in the interview itself, ~24:07) that leans on “we make a product, we sell it” simplicity.

Within that context, the guest’s own claim that AI tooling could roughly halve a fractional operations contractor’s weekly hours (12 to 6; ~12:16, E055) is, if accurate, a genuine capital-efficiency signal worth institutionalizing rather than treating as a one-time win — but it is self-reported and unaudited, so it should be treated as a hypothesis pending validation, not a baseline. We are not in a position to invent revenue, headcount, or margin figures; none were supplied, and none were found in public sources. Any scalability case for a paid engagement would need Cheekbone’s own financial and channel-mix baselines (see Document requests).

04

The priority operating capability

The most concretely described capability in the conversation is customer-intelligence-and-planning built on transaction history: Jen Harper describes an exercise that took “literally 400,000 lines of data” from roughly ten years of Shopify history, run as “a strategic plan… a nine month project” with “Excel sheets and… many hours and people involved,” which she says a human team could not otherwise complete (“that’s something no human could actually do or if they did it’s going to take them nine months,” ~15:03, ~42:03; E059, E192). The stated purpose was to “truly hone in on who our actual customer is” — a persona the team calls “Nadine” — to improve targeting and, longer-term, demand planning (fractional ops hours claim, ~12:16; E055).

As an illustrative concept only: inputs would be historical transaction/purchase data (currently, per the guest’s own description, primarily Shopify/DTC); activities would be segmentation, targeting, and demand-forecasting analysis; outputs would be a customer profile used to guide marketing spend and, prospectively, production/inventory planning; human decisions would include which segments to prioritize, how much weight to give AI-generated recommendations versus founder/team judgment, and when to escalate access or security exceptions (a real example surfaced in the conversation: an employee traveling to India “couldn’t get in” and it “became flagging as a security issue,” ~20:00; E089).

What paid discovery would need to establish before any of this becomes a specification: which tool or vendor is actually in use, whether retail-channel data is incorporated or this is a DTC-only view, what validation exists behind the underlying analysis (none has been independently confirmed), and what data-governance and consent posture applies to using customer purchase history this way. This is a concept for discussion, not a completed workflow design.

05

Proprietary data and organizational intelligence

Data known to exist (per the guest’s own account, unverified in detail): roughly ten years of Shopify transaction history (“400,000 lines of data… from the last 10 years,” ~42:03; E188); demand-planning knowledge the founder describes having personally built (“I had to literally learn the entire business of like forecasting, demand planning… how many [lipsticks] we need to make every single year,” ~12:16; E053); and informal institutional knowledge about supplier and agency reliability accumulated through, by the guest’s own account, painful hiring experience (“hired someone who said that they knew how to do all those things. And then turns out they did not,” ~12:16; E051).

Data that would need to be collected, connected, or assessed: retail-channel sales data from Sephora Canada and any Thirteen Lune/J.C. Penney arrangement (not confirmed to be integrated with the Shopify-based analysis); ingredient-level substantiation records for “clean,” silicone-free, petroleum-free, and biodegradable claims (not confirmed to exist in documented form); and a current organizational map of who holds which undocumented knowledge, given the guest’s own description of “massive changes over the last couple of years” in staffing.

06

Customer, community, and ecosystem intelligence

Cheekbone presents itself, on its own site, as built around Indigenous community relationship and reciprocity: “Drawing from Indigenous teachings and Jenn’s Indigenous roots, our products are sustainable, high-quality, clean, vegan, and cruelty-free… we make every effort to use only what’s needed for the least amount of environmental impact” (cheekbonebeauty.com/pages/about), and it operates a scholarship fund with “more than $200,000” donated to date “to a wide variety of causes” (cheekbonebeauty.com/pages/about). B Lab’s public assessment shows Cheekbone’s strongest subscore is Community (41.5 of the section’s scale, including a “Designed to Give” score of 22.7), well above its Environment (10.0) and Customers (1.0) subscores (bcorporation.net, accessed 2026; Certified Since March 2022, Overall B Impact Score 86.6 vs. a median of 50.9). That pattern — strong on community/giving design, comparatively thin on the formal “Customers” stewardship category B Lab tracks (data privacy, feedback channels, ethical marketing) — is worth naming as an area for discovery, not assumed as a weakness, since B Lab’s public page does not explain the gap.

We found no evidence, and no client statement, of a formal customer or community advisory panel, so this section should not assume one exists. Any customer feedback loop beyond purchase-transaction data (the “Nadine” analysis) would need explicit consent and ownership terms established before being built into a repeatable process.

07

Human capability and governance

The conversation itself models something worth naming directly: the founder’s own, unprompted self-assessment that “the biggest challenge over the years is truthfully been just me, my lack of experience,” and “I’ve just been probably the biggest roadblock” (transcript, ~03:53; E010, E011, E023). That is a strength — self-awareness that precedes a deliberate move toward better team composition — and it is also precisely the kind of judgment, relationship, and accountability structure that should stay human-led through any transition, not be delegated to a tool.

Grounded only in what Shane James describes as Be Human’s own working style (Section 0): a potential engagement’s discovery phase could reasonably start where Be Human says it starts elsewhere — with values alignment and organizational readiness before any software or AI-tooling decision (transcript, ~17:59, ~38:31), and with attention to psychological safety for a team that has already been through “massive changes… over the last couple of years”. We are not asserting Be Human has already scoped or committed to specific deliverables for Cheekbone; the host’s statements describe his general practice with other clients, not a commitment made in this conversation.

08

Recommended sequence and measures of value

An illustrative path only, not a committed roadmap:

  1. Paid discovery and baseline measurement: establish which claims can be substantiated internally (ingredient documentation, AI/data-tooling detail, succession-planning status, channel-level sales data) — see Document requests.
  2. Validate the priority capability: confirm what the customer-segmentation and ops-automation work actually covers (channels, vendor, governance) before treating it as a scaled system.
  3. Final blueprint: produced only after the client subscribes or pays for the engagement, incorporating validated findings from steps 1–2.
  4. Possible implementation and evaluation: subject to agreed scope not yet defined here.

Candidate measures of value to discuss in discovery (illustrative, not committed): share of “clean”/biodegradable claims with documented substantiation; whether customer segmentation incorporates retail-channel data; whether a documented succession or knowledge-transfer plan exists; and change in remote-access security incidents (the India-access example, ~20:00, being one data point already on record).

Key open questions for discovery: What does “10 years” and “12 years developing color formulas” actually reconcile to internally? What vendor and data scope underlie the “400,000 lines of data” claim? Is there a documented CEO-search process, or is this still an intention? What retail-partner data-sharing terms exist?

09 — The future-state thesis and strategic question

As Cheekbone extends beyond color cosmetics into skincare, beyond a single sales channel into omnichannel retail, and potentially beyond founder-led leadership, which of those three transitions — category, channel, or leadership — most needs a documented governance structure first, and what would need to be true internally to know?

These signals point toward an organization that could, with deliberate work, carry its founder-built trust and Indigenous-rooted positioning into a second product category (skincare) and a genuinely multi-channel retail footprint — without that expansion outrunning its ability to substantiate claims, govern its data, or transfer institutional knowledge beyond one person. We are not promising this outcome; it depends on validation this preliminary package cannot perform.

Next step: We’d welcome the chance to discuss these questions directly with you as part of a paid Be Human engagement, starting with the discovery work in Section 8 aimed at the leadership-succession and AI/data-governance opportunity in Section 2. As above, the final blueprint is a separate deliverable produced only after you subscribe or pay for that engagement — this document is a demonstration of the kind of source-grounded thinking that engagement would build on, not the blueprint itself.

Work With Be Human AI →

10

Assumptions and questions to validate

Naming variant (not a factual dispute): the transcript and notes render the founder’s name “Jen Harper”; independent company, press, B Corp, and financial-partner sources consistently render it “Jenn Harper” (e.g., cheekbonebeauty.com, glossy.co 2023-04-13, bmo.com). Treated here as a spelling variant of the same person, not corrected in the source material.

V008 — “10 years” vs. documented founding history: guest states Cheekbone “will celebrate 10 years of business this November [2024]” and separately “10 years in” (transcript, ~15:03, ~46:49), while she also states elsewhere in the same conversation “we launched in 2016” and multiple independent sources place the official launch in November 2016 (glossy.co 2023-04-13; ised-isde.canada.ca 2021-07-04; chatelaine.com 2022-04-19). November 2024 from a November 2016 launch is eight years; from the January 2015 origin story it is closer to nine years, ten months. The supplied conversation is an episode of a podcast hosted by Shane James, who describes the venture behind it as “the be human company” (transcript:cheekbone-beauty-jen-harper.txt, Shane James, ~17:59: “I need to know their values and where they’re going to be with match with the be human Right.”). Shane James also frames the guiding principle as redesigning “the organization around what humans and machines are uniquely good at” rather than treating AI as another software purchase. html:
THE BE HUMAN COMPANY

Strategic intelligence · Preliminary · 2026-09-14

Strategic intelligence — preliminary outside-in blueprint

Nova Skin & Wellness Centre

An integrated aesthetics-wellness-hormone clinic built by one founder’s vision is entering a fast-growing, increasingly crowded Vancouver longevity market; the next five years likely turn on whether that vision can scale into a team-and-brand system without diluting the human-led care experience patients say they came for.

Prepared for

Dr. Mona Garhar, Founder & Medical Director, Nova Skin & Wellness Centre

Prepared by

The Be Human Company

Assessment date

2026-09-14

Status

Preliminary. Not the final blueprint.

Demonstrate the strategic value of a Be Human engagement by exploring how Nova Skin & Wellness Centre could turn its integrated whole-body care model and vision-led hiring philosophy into a durable, scalable, human-centered growth system as it pursues Dr. Garhar’s stated five-year goals.

This preliminary blueprint demonstration draws on the supplied conversation and selected external research. It offers an initial view of opportunities we could explore together. The final blueprint is developed separately once you subscribe or pay for an engagement with The Be Human Company. The ideas here remain preliminary and require internal discovery and validation. Nothing in this document — including any later human review or editing of this draft — constitutes the final blueprint.

01

The strategic window

Dr. Garhar told podcast host Shane James that Nova Skin & Wellness Centre exists to fix a specific gap she saw as a working clinician: patients moving between disconnected providers for cosmetic treatment, hormone care, and general wellness. “You would have your patient coming for like a cosmetic treatment and then they would go somewhere else and do their wellness or their hormones. It just didn’t quite feel right.” (transcript ~18:33; E057). Her response was to build one clinic offering “aesthetics… wellness… hormones, weight loss, lasers” under a single roof (transcript ~04:39; E009), with the explicit goal that “a client or a person [doesn’t] need to go to all of these isolated areas when they can just get all of that care in the same building” (transcript ~18:33; E062).

That founder-stated thesis is now consistent with independently documented market movement, though the two are not the same kind of evidence. What the conversation establishes (client-stated, not independently verified): the clinic is roughly one year old at the time of recording, self-funded with no co-founders or investors, and currently staffed by four to five people (transcript ~04:39, ~11:51; E011, E028) — a very early-stage operation by her own account. What fresh research independently establishes (dated, external): Canada’s medical aesthetics market was estimated at $1,196.0 million in 2025, projected to reach $2,183.2 million by 2031 at a 10.0% CAGR, with the report explicitly naming “integration with broader wellness and self-care movements” as a growth driver (MarketsandMarkets, Canada Medical Aesthetics Market, accessed 2026-09-14). Separately, PwC frames menopause care as a “$10 billion to $15 billion global market” growing 8%–10% annually through 2030, driven partly by the FDA’s 2025 removal of the black-box warning on hormone replacement therapy, which “helped reframe its risk-benefit profile, driving renewed clinical use and investment” (PwC, “Unlocking the menopause opportunity”, dated 2026-05-11). Note on dating: both of these sources carry 2026 publication metadata that appears ahead of a normal calendar; the prior client research report flagged the same anomaly across several sources, so treat the underlying dollar figures as directionally credible industry-analyst estimates rather than precisely dated facts.

Why timing matters now, specifically: the same searches that confirmed this demand trend also surfaced direct new competition entering Dr. Garhar’s own market. A U.S.-based longevity and wellness chain, Next Health, lists a “Coming Soon” location at 123 & 125 East 13th Street, North Vancouver, BC, with a founding-member waitlist already open (Next Health, Vancouver location page, accessed 2026-09-14). A second nurse-led competitor, Eterna Wellness, is already operating in Vancouver at 1401 W Broadway #800 with an almost identical positioning — “Medical Aesthetics & Longevity Clinic,” hormone health, injectables, IV therapy, all under “medical oversight” (Eterna Wellness, homepage, accessed 2026-09-14). This is a genuine signal, not a hypothesis: the integrated-aesthetics-plus-longevity category Dr. Garhar helped define for herself locally is now being entered by a well-capitalized national brand and by at least one directly comparable independent clinic in the same city, at the same time she says she wants to “build services, builder clientele, builder brand” over the next five years (transcript ~43:06; E163). The strategic window is the next 12–24 months, before positioning, membership economics, and brand differentiation harden around whichever local operators move first and most visibly.

02

Strategic opportunities inside the business

Each opportunity below traces to a specific signal from the conversation or from research, is stated as a hypothesis pending discovery, and names the dependency that would need validation before acting.

Signal: Dr. Garhar’s own description of the “aha” case — a patient arriving for acne treatment who, through consultation and bloodwork, discovers a hormonal root cause and ends up on an integrated care path (transcript ~18:33; E063) — is a strong, repeatable narrative device, but it currently lives only in her own telling, not in any documented case, outcome measure, or public asset found in this research. Implication: if a national chain (Next Health) and a local peer (Eterna Wellness) both market “integrated longevity” language, the clinic that can show — not just say — connected outcomes will differentiate. Proposed direction: explore whether patient-journey storytelling (with consent) could become a structured, repeatable brand asset rather than an anecdote. Expected benefit (hypothesis): stronger word-of-mouth and referral conversion in a market where “functional medicine” and “longevity science” language is becoming generic marketing vocabulary (a risk the prior research explicitly flagged as needing definitional clarity). Dependency to validate: whether the clinic currently tracks any outcome or satisfaction data beyond self-selected website testimonials, which the prior research noted are “self-selected marketing content, not independent evidence of care quality” (nova­skinandwellness.ca).

Signal: Dr. Garhar stated men are “silently suffering from andropause” and are rarely treated the way menopausal women now are (transcript ~21:10; E072, E073), yet the clinic’s own published service list already includes “Men’s Testosterone Therapy” (Nova Skin and Wellness, homepage) — meaning the service exists but, on her own account, the underlying patient-education and outreach problem she named has not yet been solved. Implication: this is a self-identified gap between an existing offering and market awareness, not a hypothesis invented for this report. Proposed direction: explore whether a distinct men’s-health communication and intake path (separate from the female-menopause-led brand voice) could reach an underserved population without diluting the existing feminine-coded wellness positioning visible on the clinic’s site and social presence. Expected benefit (hypothesis): incremental patient volume in a segment analysts describe as growing — testosterone replacement therapy is estimated by multiple industry trackers to be a multi-billion-dollar and growing global category (search-snippet estimates only in this research; not independently fetched, so treated as directional, not verified). Dependency: current male patient volume, referral source, and whether existing staff composition and marketing tone support a credible men’s-health sub-brand.

Signal: the clinic’s current “About Us” page states her credential as “DNP, NP” (Nova Skin and Wellness, About Us), while an older bio from her prior practice states “Mona (Mandeep) Garha, MSN, NP (F), Nurse Practitioner” (Coal Harbour Medical Clinic, team profile). The prior research report explicitly treats the DNP claim as an unverified-lead, not a confirmed fact, and recommends not stating it as settled without her confirmation. Implication: this is not evidence of wrongdoing — NP-led aesthetic practice is explicitly permitted in BC (per a BCCNM guidance snippet cited by the prior research, not independently re-fetched here) — but any growth strategy that leans on clinical authority as a brand pillar (which this one visibly does, given the “Dr.” framing throughout her marketing) carries reputational exposure if the credential story is inconsistent across public touchpoints. Proposed direction: a straightforward, proactive “how we describe our team’s credentials” page or standard could pre-empt scrutiny rather than invite it. Dependency: her own confirmation of the MSN-to-DNP progression timeline, and legal/regulatory review of BCCNM’s Use-of-Title standard, neither of which this research could independently complete.

Signal: Dr. Garhar explicitly said she is holding off on patient-facing AI because “how much can AI really replicate quality” in “patient-facing roles or just customer-facing roles” is unresolved for her (transcript ~33:17; E111, E112), and that AI-generated content strips out the “emotions and… visions and… values” that differentiate her business (transcript ~25:35; E082). Implication: this is squarely aligned with the host’s (Be Human’s) own stated positioning that “consumers are going to move to what’s more human” (transcript ~26:51; E085) — a host claim, not an independently verified market fact, but directly consistent with her own clinical instinct to “wait a little bit to see how things are going to unroll before I jump in” (transcript ~29:22; E093). Proposed direction: rather than treating her caution as something to overcome, explore packaging it as a stated policy — a visible, patient-facing commitment to keep specific care decisions human — which several of the newer, larger competitors entering her market are unlikely to lead with. Dependency: whether “humans in patient-facing roles” can be operationalized as a documented, communicable standard rather than an informal preference.

Opportunity A

Convert the integrated-care story into a defensible, communicable brand asset before competitors copy the model

Opportunity B

Build the andropause/men’s health service line she has already identified as underserved

Opportunity C

Resolve the credential and positioning ambiguity before it becomes a trust liability

Opportunity D

Treat the founder’s cautious AI stance as a marketing and governance asset, not just an operating constraint

03

The scalability and economics story

Nova currently operates as a single-location, founder-owned clinic with, by her own account, four to five staff and no external investors or co-founders (transcript ~04:39, ~11:51; E011, E028). We do not have — and this report does not invent — any figures for current revenue, patient volume at Nova specifically, or profitability; the prior research explicitly logged clinic founding date, revenue, and patient volume as unresolved gaps.

What is verifiable is the clinic’s own published economic model: a tiered membership program (Nova Founders at $550/year with Botox at $9/unit; Nova Heritage at $137/month; Nova Legacy at $410/month, each bundling recurring services like IV therapy, facials, or laser sessions) (Nova Skin and Wellness, homepage). This is a recurring-revenue structure layered on top of episodic treatment sales — a sensible foundation for capital efficiency in a single-location practice, because it converts one-time cosmetic visits into repeat, budgeted relationships without requiring new headcount for each membership sold. Whether that membership base is currently large enough to fund expansion, additional staff, or a second location is unknown from the public record; Dr. Garhar herself frames growth cautiously — “I want to have small goals” (transcript ~44:11; E167) — which is itself a meaningful signal about the pace she intends to pursue, not a constraint to be argued against.

The scalability question worth exploring in a paid engagement is not “how big can this get” but "what has to be true operationally before the current model — built around one founder’s personal clinical judgment and a four-to-five-person team — can add a second practitioner cohort, a second service pillar (e.g., men’s health), or a second location without breaking the personality-and-values-based hiring model she credits as her greatest strength (transcript ~10:59; E025). No headcount, revenue, or ROI figures are estimated here; that would need discovery-stage data the clinic itself would need to supply.

04

The priority operating capability

The single highest-priority capability implied by the conversation is the integrated-intake and cross-referral pathway — the mechanism by which a patient arriving for one concern (skin, weight, energy, mood) is recognized as a candidate for hormone, wellness, or preventative services, and vice versa. This is the mechanism Dr. Garhar describes as the clinic’s core differentiator (transcript ~18:33; E063) and it is presently, by her own account, dependent on her own clinical judgment and her front-line staff’s attentiveness rather than any documented, repeatable protocol.

Conceptually, such a capability would need: inputs (a consistent intake questionnaire or conversation prompt set that surfaces cross-domain symptoms — sleep, mood, skin, energy — regardless of which service the patient booked); activities (a practitioner or care coordinator recognizing a cross-referral opportunity and initiating the conversation, most credibly done by a clinician given the health-history sensitivity involved); outputs (a documented pattern of “here’s what else we found” conversions that could become the case-study material described in Opportunity A); and human decisions retained throughout — specifically, Dr. Garhar has already told us where she draws this line herself: she is not comfortable letting AI systems carry the actual patient-facing conversation about symptoms or care recommendations (transcript ~33:17; E111, E112), even while she is comfortable using AI for problem-solving and back-office business tasks (transcript ~24:30; E080).

This is a concept, not a completed workflow design. A paid discovery phase would need to establish what intake process exists today (paper form, EMR module, verbal-only), whether the “offered AI… as part of our operations and EMR” she mentioned but has not onboarded (transcript ~33:17; E108, E109) is still under evaluation, and what a repeatable cross-referral trigger would need to look like without ever putting a machine between a patient and a clinical judgment she has said she is not ready to delegate.

05

Proprietary data and organizational intelligence

The most valuable organizational knowledge Nova likely holds is exactly the pattern Dr. Garhar described verbally but that does not appear to exist as structured data anywhere in the public record: the recurring symptom clusters she has observed across patients (middle-aged women with sleep disruption, irritability, and fatigue at menopause; men with fatigue and mood changes from andropause — transcript ~21:10; E067, E072) and which services those patients ultimately used. This pattern-recognition currently lives in her head and her staff’s informal observation, not in a system.

What is known to exist: an EMR with an AI module offered but not yet activated (transcript ~33:17; E108). What would need to be assessed in discovery, not assumed: whether that EMR currently captures cross-service patient histories in a structured, queryable way, or whether — as is common in small clinics — different services (aesthetics bookings vs. hormone consultations vs. IV therapy) are tracked separately with limited connective data. If the latter, the clinic’s most differentiating asset — the “we discovered your acne was actually a hormone issue” pattern — is currently undocumented institutional memory, which is a fragile position for a single-founder practice planning five years of growth.

06

Customer, community, and ecosystem intelligence

Nova does not appear to have a formal patient community, advisory panel, or third-party outcome-tracking relationship based on available evidence; its public-facing “voice of customer” consists of testimonials on its own website, which the prior research correctly characterized as self-selected marketing content rather than independent evidence of care quality (Nova Skin and Wellness, homepage). This is not a criticism of the clinic — nearly all small practices operate this way — but it is a gap relative to the “life-changing” outcome claims Dr. Garhar makes in her own words (transcript ~21:10, ~43:06; E069, E165), which currently rest entirely on her own account rather than any documented or third-party-verifiable outcome measure.

One genuine ecosystem asset does exist and is independently corroborated, not self-reported: her role as an Adjunct Professor at the UBC MacIsaac School of Nursing, confirmed on UBC’s own site rather than the clinic’s marketing — “Mona Garha. Adjunct Professor. Contact Information. Email mgarha@mail.ubc.ca.” (UBC Nursing — Our People). This is a credible, non-marketing credibility anchor and a potential community/ecosystem bridge (teaching relationships, student placements, academic legitimacy) that does not appear to be actively leveraged in the clinic’s public positioning beyond a title mention. The membership tiers ($550/yr, $137/mo, $410/mo) also function as a lightweight community-retention mechanism, though whether they generate any structured feedback loop (surveys, renewal-reason data) is unknown.

07

Human capability and governance

The judgment that should clearly remain human-led — because Dr. Garhar has already said so herself — is the clinical conversation with patients about symptoms, root causes, and treatment paths (transcript ~33:17; E111, E112), and the hiring decision for anyone in a client-facing role. Her hiring standard is explicit and consistent throughout the conversation: “my biggest criteria for hiring doesn’t have to do with credentials. It has to do with your personality as a human being” (transcript ~12:19; E033), paired with a stated willingness to let go quickly of anyone with “a bad attitude” because “they will affect everybody in your practice” (transcript ~12:19; E040). This is a governance philosophy already in place, not something to be introduced — the opportunity is in making it explicit and repeatable as the team grows past four to five people, rather than remaining solely in her own judgment.

Be Human’s own stated positioning, as voiced by host Shane James in this conversation, is directly aligned here: leadership’s job is to figure out “how to get them to win” (transcript ~16:17; E051, E052), and “you can’t build a company called the human company and not start with the human” (transcript ~31:41; E104). Grounded in that seller context, Be Human’s role — if this engagement proceeds — would be to help translate Dr. Garhar’s existing, informal hiring and quality instincts into a documented governance standard: who owns the decision to introduce any AI tool into a patient-facing role (she has already said this decision point matters to her — transcript ~33:17; E110), what approval step exists before that happens, and how “quality” gets evaluated before and after. This report does not commit Be Human to any specific delivery method, tool, or timeline for that work.

08

Recommended sequence and measures of value

An illustrative path, not a committed plan: a paid discovery phase would logically start by establishing baselines that do not currently exist in the public record — current patient volume and service mix by category, current intake/referral documentation (if any), current membership retention, and a plain accounting of what “life-changing outcomes” (transcript ~43:06; E165) means in measurable terms the clinic would be comfortable tracking. From there, the final blueprint (a separate, paid deliverable) would translate the opportunities in Section 2 into a sequenced set of recommendations specific to what discovery finds.

Candidate measures of value worth discussing, subject to what the clinic can actually observe: cross-referral rate (share of single-service visits that convert to a second service line), membership renewal rate by tier, and — if the men’s-health opportunity (Opportunity B) is pursued — visit volume in that category before and after any targeted outreach. Key discovery questions include: what does the clinic’s EMR currently capture across service lines; what credential-disclosure standard exists today; and what would “small goals” (transcript ~44:11; E167) mean in Dr. Garhar’s own terms for the next 12 months specifically. No implementation dates, deliverable scope, or guaranteed outcomes are promised here; those require agreed scope in a paid engagement.

09 — The future-state thesis and strategic question

as Next Health and comparable competitors bring standardized, multi-location longevity offerings into greater Vancouver, what specifically should Nova preserve, document, and communicate about its founder-led, human-first care model so that “personal and integrated” remains a felt patient experience — not just a marketing phrase — as the clinic adds staff and, potentially, services?

If Nova Skin & Wellness Centre succeeds at the five-year ambition Dr. Garhar herself named — “builder services, builder clientele, builder brand, and really just focus on more of the wellness and the longevity space” (transcript ~43:06; E163) — it could plausibly become a recognized, human-led alternative to the larger, more capital-heavy longevity brands now entering Vancouver, precisely because its founder has already articulated (and lived) a values-first, personality-over-credentials operating philosophy that those larger entrants may struggle to replicate quickly. This is a possibility this evidence supports exploring, not an outcome this report promises.

Next step: We’d welcome the chance to discuss a paid Be Human engagement to pressure-test the opportunities above — starting with the integrated-care documentation gap (Section 2, Opportunity A) and the human-capability governance work (Section 7) — through structured discovery that produces your final blueprint.

Work With Be Human AI →

10

Assumptions and questions to validate

Educational timeline: the transcript states 11 years of university total (~03:59; E007) alongside a two-year doctorate (~01:56; E005); the arithmetic across two bachelor’s degrees, a master’s, and a doctorate was not independently reconciled. Affects only biographical framing, not the strategic recommendations above.

Credential discrepancy (central caution from prior research): the clinic’s current bio states “DNP, NP”; an older bio for the same person states “MSN, NP.” The prior research explicitly labels the DNP claim an unverified-lead. This report does not assert she holds a doctorate, and does not describe her as a physician or “MD” at any point. Any brand or governance work (Opportunity C, Section 7) depends on her resolving this directly.

Family practice vs. Nova conflation: the separate, seven-year, ~1,000-patient family practice (~00:27; E002, E004) is distinct from the newer, ~1-year-old Nova clinic (~11:51; E028); treated as two different practices per her own description, but the current relationship between the two (shared patients, staff, referral flow) was not established.

Ownership/financing: she states no co-founders, investors, or shareholders (~04:39; E011); loan or lease-financing arrangements were not addressed and do not change the recommendations above regardless of answer.

Launch timeline: the pregnancy/launch story (~04:39; E010) is used only as founder-resilience color, not as a scheduling fact for any recommendation.

Adjunct professor role: independently corroborated by UBC’s own site (a genuine credibility anchor), but the specific course, program duration, and student population remain unconfirmed and would sharpen Section 6 if resolved.

Contact details: the clinic’s stated website (NovaSkinandWellness.ca) and social handle were not independently re-verified as currently active in this run.

Binding open questions carried from prior research, not to be asserted as fact in either direction: (1) whether “published author” is supported by any specific, locatable publication — currently self-reported on Instagram only; (2) whether Dr. Garhar holds active, good-standing BCCNM registration — the registry could not be queried interactively in either research pass; (3) whether the similarly-named Calgary “Nova Skin & Wellness YYC” shares any ownership or operational relationship with the Vancouver clinic — no evidence of common ownership was found, and none should be assumed.

Market-data dating anomaly: several externally sourced market figures used in Section 1 (MarketsandMarkets, PwC) carry 2026 publication metadata that appears to be a research-environment clock artifact rather than a real future date; treat the dollar and percentage figures as directionally credible analyst estimates, not precisely dated facts.

Unresolved for a paid engagement to establish: current patient volume and revenue by service line at Nova specifically; current EMR data-capture structure; current credential-disclosure standard used with patients; current membership renewal data — none of which were available in the supplied sources or public web record.

11

Research basis and sources

This assessment draws on four supplied sources — a podcast transcript, structured evidence notes derived from that transcript, a prior client research report, and the raw evidence bundle backing that report — plus a limited amount of fresh, cited web research conducted in this task.

Direct observations (guest’s own words, not independently verified unless otherwise noted): the integrated-care model and founding rationale; the hiring philosophy; the five-year goals; the cautious approach to patient-facing AI; team size and funding structure at time of recording.

External findings (independently sourced, with URL and date where available): clinic services, positioning language, membership pricing, and team roster from the clinic’s own website; the credential discrepancy between the clinic’s current bio and a prior-practice bio; the UBC adjunct professor role, corroborated on UBC’s own site; Canada medical aesthetics and global menopause/hormone-therapy market growth figures; two named Vancouver-area competitors (Eterna Wellness, operating; Next Health, entering the market).

Estimates (search-snippet-only, not independently fetched, lower confidence): testosterone-replacement-therapy and Canada GLP-1 weight-loss-drug market sizing figures; the clinic’s exact street address.

Strategic inference (this report’s own synthesis, explicitly hypotheses, not facts): all recommendations in Section 2; the framing of AI caution as a marketing/governance asset; the future-state thesis in Section 9.

Strategic intelligence — preliminary outside-in blueprint

Nova Skin and Wellness

grow without losing the human quality of care you built it for.

Prepared for

Dr. Mona Garhar, Founder and Medical Director, Nova Skin and Wellness Centre

Prepared by

The Be Human Company

Assessment date

2026-09-21

Status

Preliminary. Not the final blueprint.

Demonstrate how a paid Be Human engagement could help Nova identify and prioritise opportunities for growth, better workflows and appropriate AI support, while protecting human-led care.

This preliminary blueprint draws on the notes from our conversation. It illustrates opportunities to investigate, not confirmed findings about Nova’s operations or an implementation plan. The final blueprint is developed through a paid Be Human engagement.

01

The strategic window

You want to grow Nova’s services, team and reputation. You also want patients to keep experiencing the warmth and connected care that led you to build the clinic in the first place.

Those ambitions belong together. The question is where better workflows and carefully chosen AI support could make growth easier—without compromising clinical judgement or the patient relationships your team has built.

This preliminary view shows where we would begin. Through a paid Be Human engagement, we would examine the opportunities against Nova’s operations and develop your final blueprint: what to prioritise, where technology belongs, and what should remain human-led.

02

Strategic opportunities inside the business

Start with the work around the care

You described wanting patients to receive connected care rather than move between isolated services. You also raised a clear concern about AI: whether it could match the quality your front-line staff already provide.

We would start with the work around that experience: how an enquiry becomes an appointment, how information reaches the right person, and how the team follows up. Discovery would establish where friction exists and whether better workflows—with or without AI—could reduce administrative effort while preserving personal attention.

03

The scalability and economics story

Give yourself more room to lead Nova

How much of your time should Nova’s next stage require? We would look for ways to give you more room to lead it.

We would distinguish decisions that need your clinical judgement from those that need your direction as a founder—and tasks your team could handle with clearer responsibilities, better information or appropriate AI support. The aim is to focus your involvement where it matters, not remove you from the patient relationships you value.

If routine coordination or administration is taking time you would rather spend with patients, developing your team or planning Nova’s next stage, we would assess what could change and whether the time returned would justify the investment.

04

The priority operating capability

Let AI prepare the response. Keep your team in the conversation.

A prospective patient asks which services Nova offers and how to arrange a consultation. An AI assistant could prepare a reply using information your team has approved—service descriptions, booking steps and clinic policies—so a staff member can check, personalise and send it rather than start from a blank page.

Questions about symptoms, treatment suitability or medical history would stay outside that task. They would go to the appropriate member of your team, not receive an automated clinical answer.

If routine enquiries are reaching you today, this could be one way to give you time back. We would assess their volume, how they are handled and whether a privacy-appropriate setup could reduce drafting time and unnecessary escalations. If the benefit is too small, we would recommend a simpler change.

05

Proprietary data and organisational intelligence

Make Nova’s knowledge easier for your team to use

For an assistant to prepare useful replies, it needs more than a description of your services. It needs the information your team is comfortable standing behind: how consultations are booked, what patients should expect, and when a question needs someone’s judgement.

We would establish what guidance already exists and what still relies on asking you or an experienced colleague. Making that knowledge easier to find could help your team before AI is introduced.

The starting point would be approved service and administrative information—not patient records. We would assess what belongs in that knowledge base, who maintains it, and how staff can recognise when an answer needs escalation.

06

Customer, community, and ecosystem intelligence

Learn from the questions people ask

Repeated enquiries may reveal where people are unsure about Nova’s services, what a consultation involves, or how to take the next step.

We would look for those patterns without bringing identifiable patient details into an exploratory AI tool. Where the evidence supports it, clearer website information, booking guidance or staff responses could answer common questions earlier and reduce avoidable back-and-forth.

That gives us a second measure of value: whether prospective patients find it easier to understand Nova and arrange a consultation, not just whether replies take less time.

07

Human capability and governance

Support your team without making yourself the help desk

You described looking for people who are open to feedback and learning. Any new way of working should build on that strength—not leave staff uncertain about when to trust a tool or when to ask you.

We would work through the responsibilities as well as the technology: who checks a drafted response, which questions go to a clinician, and who keeps the approved information current. Staff would need clear guidance for correcting an answer or choosing not to use it.

A workflow that saves drafting time but adds more checking and interruptions for you may not be worthwhile. We would account for that supervision before recommending it.

08

Recommended sequence and measures of value

A clear decision before a technology commitment

The engagement turns these opportunities into a prioritised plan. For enquiry support, the work would follow three steps:

Understand the work. Establish how enquiries are handled today, where your time is involved, and what information and systems the team already uses.

Assess the options. Compare clearer guidance, changes to responsibilities and AI-assisted drafting. We would weigh the potential time returned against cost, privacy requirements and the effort needed to supervise each option.

Develop the final blueprint. Recommend what to prioritise, explain the reasoning, and identify the responsibilities and measures needed for a sensible next step. Any implementation would be separately scoped and agreed.

Success needs to show up in the working day—not just a demonstration. Useful measures could include your time on routine escalations, staff time per enquiry, corrections needed to drafted replies, and the accuracy and timeliness of patient information.

09 — The future-state thesis and strategic question

Where could better support give you time back without taking you away from the work and relationships you want to keep?

Build Nova’s next stage with more room to lead

Better support could give your team more room to act and you more room to lead, without making Nova less personal. Your final blueprint would help you decide where that is achievable and whether AI belongs in the solution.

Purchase your Be Human engagement through this portal to develop Nova’s final blueprint. We’ll use the paid work to examine these opportunities against your operations and recommend a practical way forward. If you have questions about the scope before purchasing, speak with us first.

Work With Be Human AI →

10

Assumptions and questions to validate

What we would establish with you

Before recommending a change, we would establish:

You do not need to answer these questions before purchasing. Investigating them is part of the engagement.

Where your time goes: which routine questions reach you, how often, and which you would prefer your team to handle.

Whether the task is worth improving: enquiry volumes, response effort and the effect of interruptions on your working day.

What already works: the guidance, responsibilities and systems your team relies on today.

What the boundaries require: what information could be used, who would review outputs, and which questions must remain with qualified staff.

Whether the benefit justifies the effort: the likely time returned, ongoing supervision and costs.

11

Research basis and sources

What this preliminary view is based on

This blueprint is based on the notes from your conversation with Shane James, with transcript references available to clarify the points carried forward:

  • Your growth ambitions: developing Nova’s services, clientele, brand and team.
  • Your approach to care: connecting services rather than treating them in isolation.
  • Your expectations of AI: protecting the quality of the patient-facing experience when considering new systems.
  • Your approach to hiring: valuing openness to feedback and learning.

The enquiry-support example is our proposal to investigate—not a gap you reported. We have not reviewed Nova’s internal enquiry records, operating costs or workflows and make no quantified claim about time savings or financial return.
